subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CHANGES IN REGULATIONS TO PERMIT GREATER COMPETITION BETWEEN CARRIERS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the existence of restrictive regulations by the Canadian Transport Commission seriously limiting domestic and international scheduling in Canada by air carriers other than Air Canada and in view of the statements of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) both inside and out of this House that he was prepared to remove or amend these restrictive regulations, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
That this House direct the Minister of Transport to immediately make a statement on motions outlining the particulars of changes to be made to regulations of the Canadian Transport Commission to facilitate reasonable competition with Air Canada by other carriers.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INTEREST FREE LOANS TO HOUSE BUILDERS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to discuss an important matter of pressing necessity.
Since interest rates are mainly responsible for higher housing costs in Canada and considering that it has become urgent to reduce those excessive interest rates to make the purchase of a house financially attractive to every Canadian and as the federal government has already taken the first step by introducing a bill aimed at granting assistance under the form of an interest-free loan during the first five years, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte):
That the federal government take the necessary steps so that the assistance granted under the form of a loan free of interest during the first five years be extended to the duration of the loan.

subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-POSITION OF PROVINCES ON ACCEPTANCE OF FEDERAL GUIDELINES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a question to the Minister of Finance with regard to the acceptance by the provinces of the federal guidelines relating to the anti-inflation program. The minister having been unable to give the House any assurance that the Province of Quebec will follow the federal guidelines within the jurisdiction the province is reserving to itself for its own administration, can the hon. gentleman give us any assurance with respect to the Province of Saskatchewan, for example, where the Speech from the Throne appeared to indicate that the government of Saskatchewan might want certain modifications? told the House last week, there is to be a meeting of officials of the federal and provincial governments substantially on the question of the guideline program tomorrow and the next day. speechtext: May I ask whether the government is presenting to this House, to the country and to the premiers of the provinces a uniform program to be applied across Canada, a program which involves the acceptance of the same guidelines in all the provinces? apply. With regard to the public sector, we have given the provinces the option whether or not they will choose, as Ontario has, to put the administration of the public sector under the federal government body or whether they will choose their own.

subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-DIFFERENCE BETWEEN INCREASES IN WAGES AND PRICES OF PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister has just stated that a supplementary monetary benefit would amount to 52 per cent. If the 52 per cent increase becomes effective, it fully and directly comes under the cost of goods. After deduction of personal income tax at a 30 per cent rate, the real increase is only 37 per cent to pay for the 52 per cent added to prices. So how does the Prime Minister expect workers to keep up with prices in Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-DIFFERENCE BETWEEN INCREASES IN WAGES AND PRICES OF PRODUCTS
speechtext: This will be achieved in a very simple manner, Mr. Speaker. When we propose in the forthcoming year salary hikes of 8 per cent plus 2 per cent, these 8 per cent are in fact a cost of living increase. The 8 per cent are equivalent to what we expect the Consumer Price Index will be next year. We have indicated that if the CPI is more than 8 per cent, we should allow wage-earners to catch up. All the cost increases about which the hon. member is rightly concerned, are therefore included in the consumer price index and authorized accordingly under the basic formula proposed by the Minister of Finance.

subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-DIFFERENCE BETWEEN INCREASES IN WAGES AND PRICES OF PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
I am afraid the Prime Minister does not understand what I mean. Once the government allows that increase in the worker's salary, that is 8 per cent, plus 2 per cent, that total is added to the cost price of goods without, by so doing,
November 18, 1975

creating any profit since industry will not be allowed to make any profit. But the government will continue to levy income tax on the increase of 8 per cent plus 2 per cent. So, if income tax is levied at 30 per cent or 20 per cent, which the worker does not have, he still has to pay the cost price of goods which includes the total amount. According to the government's formula, how will the worker manage to pay those prices?

subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-DIFFERENCE BETWEEN INCREASES IN WAGES AND PRICES OF PRODUCTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understand the hon. member's question better. My reply is that, obviously, the matter of income tax is not taken into account, as the leader of the Social Credit Party indicates, in the formula of the government. But that also applies to all members of our society who have to pay income tax. In the case, for instance, of those who live off dividends, and not among the wealthiest, we tell them that dividends will not increase this year that does not mean they will not have to pay higher prices and income tax. So, once again, Mr. Speaker, our anti-inflation formula is not intended to free the people of their responsibility of paying taxes to the government, on every level; it is meant to control the inflationary spiral, and that is what we mean to do.

subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-DIFFERENCE BETWEEN INCREASES IN WAGES AND PRICES OF PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask another supplementary question.
The prime minister does not seem to grasp my point. When the 8, 2 and 2 per cent increase within the guidelines is added to prices, the businessman is not a entitled to a profit according to the government's basic data, therefore, how could he pay taxes on non-profit activities? The industrialist or manufacturer will not since we are dealing with cost price, while the wage-earner will pay taxes on his 8, 2, 2 per cent salary increases. What does the government suggest in such a case?

This is getting technical, Mr. Speaker, but I believe I can answer the hon. member's question. When we say 8 and 2 per cent, this means the wage-earner will be able to receive an increment of 12 per cent, for example, since the costs have increased by 8. Yes, Mr. Speaker, the salary increase is 8 per cent, the other 2 per cent concern productivity and the remaining 2 per cent are for catching up.
Therefore, according to the hon. member's own argument, salaries went up by 8 plus 4 per cent while prices went up only by 8, therefore the hon. member will get 12 per cent to purchase something which went up by 8. That means he will be ahead.

subsubtopic: APPLICATION FOR NEW TRIAL IN CASE OF KEITH LATTA- GOVERNMENT POSITION

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE RATE OF RETURN ON GOVERNMENT ANNUITY CONTRACTS
speechtext:
that Bill C-75, to increase the rate of return on government annuity contracts, to increase their flexibility and to discontinue future sales thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the 67 years since its inception, the Government Annuities Act has given Canadians some guarantee of financial security for their old age. The other day the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) told me this act was given second reading the day he was born.
The benefits provided by the annuities program filled an important void in those early days when there was an obvious lack of retirement plans and programs. We have to remember that we did not then have old age pensions, the Canada Pension Plan or the many private pension plans we have today. Due to the many initiatives undertaken by governments and the private sector, we have come a long way since then toward ensuring the basic economic welfare of the retired citizen. During the past decade, various government and private pension plans have been developed and are constantly being revised to keep pace with the demands of changing circumstances. It was with these considerations in mind that the government announced its intention in the last budget to introduce the bill which is now before us.

This act, called the Government Annuities Improvement Act, will, among other things, increase the rate of return on government annuity contracts to 7 per cent per annum, increase the range of their flexibility and discontinue future sales of annuity contracts. It will bring government annuity contracts up to date so that present annuity contract holders-there are some 280,000 of them-will no longer be subjected to the relative disadvantages of the present contract interest rate structure which varies from 3 per cent to 514 per cent. Raising the interest rate to 7 per cent brings their rate of return closer in line with rates offered in the private sector.
I would like to emphasize, however, that the annuities account should be regarded as an investment portfolio accumulated over the years where interest rates could vary from 4 per cent to the current 9 per cent or 10 per cent. The average yield would be situated somewhere between these two extremes. Consequently, the 7 per cent rate is based on a close study of the current yield on various public and private investment portfolios.
Our objective was to determine a rate of return in line with comparative investment yields and one that can be expected to remain current for some time. For example, if you examine the average yield on composite funds of life insurance companies operating in Canada, you will find that in 1974 it ranged from 7.1 per cent to 7.8 per cent. To be on a comparable basis with the government annuities where the government pays the cost of administration, these figures should be reduced by one-half per cent for administration expenses to 6.6 per cent from 7.3 per cent.
Even if you project these figures upward for 1975 by 0.2 per cent to 0.3 per cent, members will note that the 7 per cent rate proposed in this act is still in line and is even somewhat above the average rate of 6.5 per cent on the total national debt and the effective yield of 6.8 per cent on the government superannuation account. Though a 7 per cent rate is reasonable by current standards, it must be easily adjustable in the future. Accordingly, the rate of return will be subject to periodic review depending on future fluctuations in interest rates.
Let me give a few details about how the new rate will be applied to both matured and unmatured contracts in order to illustrate the effect of the change. For the 106,000 persons with matured contracts, the contract rates presently range from 3 per cent to 5!4 per cent, and percentage increases in actual payments under this act would range from 32 per cent to 10 per cent, respectively. The average percentage increase in annuity payments would be approximately 22 per cent. Because the new rate is retroactive to April 1, 1975, it will mean there will be a back payment for holders of matured annuities.
There are about 175,000 persons with deferred contracts valued at $640 million, that is, with contracts that have not yet matured. From April 1, 1975, these contracts will earn 7 per cent on the accumulated premiums and interest. For most contracts, the annuity at maturity will be increased accordingly. However, in the case of about 150 pension plans covering some 45,000 persons, the allocation of the increase must be decided by the terms of the plan itself.
November 18, 1975

To illustrate the effect if the increased interest rate is maintained, we can take the example of 4 per cent contracts not covered by special pension plan arrangements: there would be a 33 per cent increase in the annuity if it matures in ten years and a 77 per cent increase if it matures in 20 years. In addition, at maturity the annuity payment would also be increased in the same way as for the matured contracts.
One consequence of these changes is the need to raise the current $1,200 ceiling on annual annuity payments in order to accommodate the effects of the increased interest rate. This, too, as hon. members will note, is provided for in the bill. The cost of the 7 per cent increase in the rate of return is estimated to be an additional $38 million for the 1975-76 fiscal year, but we have estimated that the total additional cost to the government will slowly decrease in future years as more annuities mature.
The second major aspect of the bill reflects the proposal that no further annuity contracts will be sold after the act comes into effect. This will apply immediately to individual and group contracts. However, new registrations would be allowed covering existing employer-sponsored group contracts during the three years ending March 31, 1979, to give employers adequate time in which to make alternate arrangements with the private sector.
Our decision to cease further sales of annuity contracts is not based simply on the confidence we have in the servicing abilities of private and public institutions. More fundamentally, it springs from recognition and acceptance of the reality that average yearly sales of government annuities have been decreasing steadily over the past 27 years to a point at which only 11 new contracts were sold last year. Obviously, other public and private enterprises have been doing their job reasonably well and the need for a government program of this type has largely disappeared. Nevertheless, as I indicated earlier, we shall continue to administer existing contracts, and that will take us well into the twenty-first century because of the unelapsed time applying to so many of them.
The bill also provides for a number of housekeeping changes; some solutions which have been developed to deal with problems which have arisen in the past. By and large, these changes are self-explanatory, though I shall be glad to deal with them in more detail if requested during the committee stage.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, I call your attention to the fact that this step to enrich annuities is unprecedented and it is not legally required of the government. There are many people who have some part of their investments locked into low-interest rate bonds, mortgages, and so on. Nevertheless, I think we all agree that government annuities are a special case. No one could have foreseen the current interest rates at the time the contracts were entered into, and the government now intends to protect in this fashion the investments of those individuals who had the foresight to provide for their retirement.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE RATE OF RETURN ON GOVERNMENT ANNUITY CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill arose out of an announcement in the June 23 budget that legislation would be introduced to increase the interest paid on government annuities held by some 270,000
Government Annuities
Canadians. We welcomed this announcement in the June 23 budget. It was probably the only item in that budget which I sensed was universally accepted. It was the least the government could do for these persons, the thousands of Canadians who over the years had purchased government annuities in good faith, with the idea in mind that those annuities would yield a secure return on the investment and provide a source of income when they had left the work force.
I commend the government for taking action to recognize the needs of those who hold these annuities. Over the years during which these annuities have been offered for sale-that is, from 1908 to the present-the interest rate ran from 3 per cent to a maximum of 514 per cent. That is not a very dramatic increase over a span of 67 years. During that period, thousands of individuals purchased annuities to provide for their retirement and employers purchased them as a means of providing pensions for their employees. Most of those individuals, and all the pension funds with substantial holdings of annuities, have been in severe financial difficulty for a number of years. I believe it is worth noting that 82 per cent of the premiums received from individual annuity contract holders were deposited under registered retirement savings plan contracts.
I hope the action the government is proposing is a prelude to similar action in accordance with a formula designed to alleviate the plight of holders of perpetual government bonds. Many of these unfortunate individuals purchased perpetual bonds on the understanding that when the last coupon was clipped the bonds would be called. However, this was not done. All we heard from the government was the announcement that perpetual bonds would be redeemed by 1990. Mr. Speaker, these bonds would yield only 30 per cent of their face value if sold today. I urge the government to develop a conversion plan for them as soon as possible, thereby ending this rough justice.
We do not intend, Mr. Speaker, to take up much time of the House debating the bill before us. Three or four of my hon. friends will probably wish to take part in the discussion, but it would be our desire to have the bill sent to the committee of the whole for consideration there. I gather, though, that we cannot get the consent of all parties to such a course.
There are some matters, though, which we feel the minister might explain. For instance, we would like to know how the cost of the increased interest will be shown in the estimates. It has to be presented somewhere, of course. We should also like the position of short-term government employees clarified. We want to know what is intended to replace the system which has operated in the past under which they have converted these annuities, and the course of action they might be allowed to take.
As I say, we do not intend to take up much time on this bill. We are prepared to see it pass all stages today and I hope others taking part in the debate share this view. Thus we may alleviate the plight of these people. I am sure hon. members on all sides of the House throughout the past few years have had letters and communications from constituents of theirs explaining their plight. Many of these people are school teachers, clergymen, pension fund holders, all of

November 18, 1975
Government Annuities
whom have explained the difficulty that they are having funding their pensions with the low rate of return on government annuities.
I commend the minister and the government for bringing in the bill and I urge them to act with all speed. Let us get the bill through committee in proper order and return it to the House so it can be passed with all possible haste.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE RATE OF RETURN ON GOVERNMENT ANNUITY CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister has already indicated, and as I have mentioned on one or two previous occasions, I have a lifelong interest in this legislation. However, it is not quite as long a time as my hon. friend in the back row is suggesting. It so happens that on the very day I was born, June 18, 1908, the House of Commons debated second reading and then passed through committee on the whole the bill which we know as the Government Annuities Act. Those who made up the House of Commons of that day were divided among members who thought they were getting into an area that was no business of government, and members who were proud of the fact that the government was taking a step to assist Canadians in providing for their old age.
The maximum amount of annuity that was payable under the original act which was given second reading on June 18, 1908, was $50 a month. We have come a long way since then, in many respects. The minister correctly pointed out that this legislation over the last 67 years has enabled many people to provide themselves with a measure of security in their old age. The legislation has made this possible not only through the purchase by individuals of contracts; it has also made it possible for many employers to set up employee pensions plans under the aegis of the Government Annuities Act. Therefore, I stand here today, 67 years later, and salute the members of the House of Commons who on June 18, 1908 brought this legislation into being.
Like the hon. member who preceded me, I welcome the fact that this Government Annuities Improvement Act is going to make certain improvements in Canadian government annuities. I shall have something to say on the other side of the coin in a moment or two, but first I warmly welcome the fact that for many holders of government annuities and for many persons who are receiving payments on their government annuity contracts it will be good news to hear that their payments are going to be increased.
As I understand it from the schedule attached to the bill, a schedule that is referred to in clause 5, the increases that recipients of government annuity payments can anticipate run as follows. If one is drawing payments from a contract that was based on a return of 514 per cent, the increase in those payments will be 10 per cent. If the contract was based on a 5 per cent rate, the increase in the payments will be 14 per cent. If the contract was based on a 4 per cent interest rate, the increase in the payments over what is now being received will be 22 per cent. A contract that was issued when the rate was 3 Vi per cent will give, now, an increase in the payments of 29 per cent. And, down at the bottom, if a person had a contract that was issued when

the rate was only 3 per cent, the increase he will now receive in his annuity payments will be 32 per cent.
It is also to be noted that these payments are to be retroactive to April 1 of this year. I share the hope of the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) that this bill will not take an undue amount of time to get through, but it will not really have any effect on the amount of money the recipients of these payments will receive because whenever the bill does go through the payments will be retroactive to April 1. Also, of course, the recipients will have to wait for the postal strike to end before they get their cheques anyway. In any case, we of the House of Commons of 1975 are making a significant improvement in the legislation that was passed by the House of Commons in 1908.
May I add to what was said by the previous speaker to the effect that although the minister was justified in saying that the government was not legally required to increase payments under the Government Annuities Act, the government was morally required to do so. When the government established the principle of escalation with respect to old age security, the guaranteed income supplement, veterans' pensions and allowances, judges' pensions, members of parliament pensions, and on down the line, and then added a bonus in certain cases to payments made on Canada savings bonds, it seemed to me that the government was dragging its heels by not taking action to increase payments made under the Government Annuities Act.
I agree with the comment already made that once this has been passed, something equally worth while ought to be done with respect to those perpetual bonds of 1936. I join with all those who have said that the act of the government in declaring that these bonds will finally be called in 1996, I think it is, which is recognition that they cannot go on forever, does not really answer the problem for those who have held these bonds for a long time. There are these other matters that ought to be attended to, but at the moment we are discussing the Canadian government annuities program and the provision under which there will be the increased payments by the percentages to which I have already referred. This is a decision of the government that the House welcomes and which I am sure we will support unanimously.
The other side of the coin-I should say this right away- is that although these improvements sound fairly good when reading them out, the result is that the persons on these annuities will again be put on a fixed income basis so far as their government annuity contracts are concerned. It took us a long while to win the point that retirement income should at least be geared to the rise in the cost of living, but I go further and say that it should be geared to the rise in the standard of living or rise in the gross national product. At least we have it geared to the rise in the cost of living, and that is reflected in old age security, the guaranteed income supplement payments and all the other payments I mentioned a moment ago.
I contend that the same should apply in respect of government annuities. I noticed that the minister made no reference to these increases being related in any way to the
November 18, 1975

rise in the cost of living. He based it entirely on what has happened to interest rates over the years. The fact is that those who have government annuity contracts and are drawing payments under those contracts are persons who are drawing them as part of their provision for their retirement years. It really hits older people very hard when the cost of living goes up and only some of the elements of their income are escalated. I think the return from government annuities ought to be treated in the same way as other forms of retirement income and a formula should be devised for the increase to take place every year in accordance at least with the rise in the cost of living. Every time I say that, I feel I must get in my point that it should be in respect of the rise in the standard of living. But we have not reached that yet; that is one of the goals we still must attain.
Indeed, this action reminds me of something that was done by the Parliament of Canada in respect of retired public servants. For many years, and I mean many years- decades, in fact-we tried hard to get an increase in the pensions paid to retired public servants. The first move in that direction was made during the parliament of 1958 to 1962 when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was prime minister. I hope the fact that what I shall say in a moment will be partly critical and will not offend my friends to the right. The fact is, that government made the first move in doing something to increase the pensions of retired public servants, and it was a good first step but it was a one-shot move. All that happened under the bill that was passed during the days of that Conservative administration was the inclusion of a provision to add a percentage to the income of retired public servants.
It was most welcomed when those retired public servants got it, but a year later, two years later or three years later they found that the situation was worsening again, so the day came in about 1969 or 1970 when the Liberal government was finally persuaded that it ought to go not just for a one-shot increase in the pensions of retired public servants but ought to establish a formula for those pensions to go up year after year in accordance with the rise in the cost of living.
I submit that the same thing is happening again. Here we have the present government doing what the Conservative government did in about 1959 or 1960, bringing in a one-shot increase in payments payable under the Government Annuities Act. But it is not finishing the job. I suggest that these payments should be put on a basis so that they will escalate, just the same as other forms of retirement payments escalate under various provisions we have made.
That is the main criticism I make of this bill. Welcome though it is, and generous though this increase may sound, if you are at the bottom of one pile and the top of the other, or vice versa, that is it: you get that increase, and the new rate that you get from your government annuity stays at that rate for the rest of your life. That is not good enough, and no one should know it better than this government because this government realized through experience that what the Conservative government had done for retired public servants, though welcomed at the time, was not good enough.

speechtext: That's a different thing.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE RATE OF RETURN ON GOVERNMENT ANNUITY CONTRACTS
speechtext:
I think I made it clear that I was giving the Diefenbaker government credit for having made the first move in respect of pension increases for retired public servants, but it was a one-shot move that had to be improved. We have the same situation today; we have a one-shot move and I do not think it will stand up.
When you realize the government is discontinuing the sale of government annuity contracts, it seems to me this is all the more reason it should protect the position of those who have contracts under this legislation. In that connection, Mr. Speaker, I think I should go on to say that I regret the fact that the government has proposed to discontinue the issuing of contracts under the Government Annuities Act. Of course, it is not rescinding the Government Annuities Act; it will have to go on for another 50, 75 or maybe 100 years, for all I know, until all the persons who now have contracts have lived out their days. So the Government Annuities Act has to continue. But as the minister has said, once this bill is passed and becomes law, no more individual contracts will be issued except in a few cases where substitute contracts are written for those already in existence, and after March 31,	1979, no additional
employees can be enrolled in any group plans already in existence.
I suppose that one of the reasons I do not man the barricades about this and really say we should not let this part of the bill go through is, of course, the fact that the government has let the position of government annuities deteriorate in relation to other forms of retirement income that individuals or companies can purchase. That reminds me of the lobby that has gone on for years against the Canada Government Annuities Act. One has only to read the debate the day the original bill was given second reading, to which I have already referred, to note there the concern that the government might be getting into business that should be the preserve of private enterprise.
I remember with particular vividness the year 1951. We had been campaigning, quite a few of us, to get the Canada Government Annuities Act improved, and in that year the government finally agreed to take action. The minister of labour of that day-the Government Annuities Act came under the minister of labour in those days-brought in a bill to amend the Government Annuities Act, making a number of improvements, putting government annuities in a position where they would be competitive with annuities and contracts that could be purchased in the private sector.
We welcomed the bill. It was a bit of a pleasant surprise to have the government make the improvements that were included in that legislation. It came in for second reading, it was passed and referred to one of the standing committees. In those days bills did not go to standing committees automatically; the rule was to deal with them in committee of the whole and it was the exception to send a bill to a

November 18, 1975
Government Annuities
standing committee. However, this bill was sent to a standing committee.
I remember at the time wondering why it was given that treatment, but I soon discovered the reason was that there were quite a few bodies who wanted to appear and to make representations. I have never met so many insurance company heads and executives in my life, not even when we had the Canada Pension Plan before a special joint committee. They came here in force to try to persuade us that we should not proceed with that government bill which, as I say, was designed to improve the Government Annuities Act at that time.
I remember that we had a meeting of the committee one day and it looked as though we were going to lose the vote to support the bill and send it back to the House. If I can be a bit reminiscent about it, a friend of mine-he is still a friend even though he is in the other place-David Croll, was on our side and felt that this bill should be improved and we had to get it through. Between us we agreed that we just did not have the manpower in the committee, at that meeting, to win the vote se we managed to keep it going until adjournment time in order to get another meeting of the committee. David Croll assured me that there were members like the late Lionel Conacher and others on the Liberal side who were not attending that morning but whom he would get to the later meeting and we would win.
Sure enough, when we met the next time all the members were there and we carried the day. The bill was passed in the committee and was referred back to the House. But that was the end of it. It was reported back to the House for third reading, and when we asked the minister when we would have third reading we received no satisfaction. In other words, the insurance lobby had persuaded the government not to go ahead with the 1951 bill that would have improved the Government Annuities Act.
The minister says today that the number of sales of contracts has been dropping over the last 25 years. Well, I have been reciting something that happened 24 years ago. It is true that because government annuities have been allowed to deteriorate, the number of persons wanting to buy them has gone down greatly. That, of course, I suppose is the reason they are now to be discontinued altogether. I think this is unfortunate. I believe it would have been better to make further improvements to the Government Annuities Act so that persons who do not feel they are providing enough for their retirement through old age security, the Canada Pension Plan and other pension arrangements, could invest in their government through Canadian government annuities.
I regret very much that the ground has been prepared during these 20-odd years for the day when there would seem to be no case for continuing the sale of Canadian government annuities. So, Mr. Speaker, I regret that there are those clauses in the bill that will discontinue the sale of individual contracts and will provide for there to be no more registrations of employees, even in existing group contracts, after March 31, 1979.
The minister suggested today that this legislation over these past 67 years has helped a lot of people make provision for their old age. I agree. But the fact is that we now

have other arrangements. We have old age security, the guaranteed income supplement, the Canada Pension Plan and many more employee pension plans both in the public and the private sector, and therefore the need for this now is not as great as it was in 1908 or in many of the years that followed. I agree. But if the government wishes to boast about the provisions that have been made and tell us how wonderful it is that we have the Old Age Security Act, the Canada Pension Plan and retirement pension plans for public servants, members of the RCMP and members of the armed forces, and so on, I submit the government is morally obligated to see to it that those programs are put on the best possible basis.
Today I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) whether the government intended to do anything in this session about the basic amount of old age security. I received his stock answer which was no answer at all to my question. He reminded me, as if I do not know it, that there is a quarterly escalation of old age security.
In a supplementary question I tried to remind him that that escalation is always behind and does not relate to the goods or services older people actually have to buy, and that as yet we do not have a perfect system of security for the retirement years of our people. If the government now proposes to take away this one means of retirement income that has been there for many years, it is morally obligated to make improvements in the other forms of retirement income. Therefore, I again call for a substantial improvement in the basic amount of old age security; I call for improvement in the public service pension plan and the RCMP and armed forces plans with which we are dealing under Bill C-52 before another committee. I call for action on the part of the government to get the railways of this country to put their pension plans on a better basis. I say we should not take away something that is there until we have improved the other plans that are supposed to provide for the retirement of our people.
I shall end where I began. The debate of 1908 to which I referred is an interesting one to read. The members of that day felt they were breaking new ground to be interfering at all in the provision of old age retirement. Some members were concerned. I have not taken the time to read what Their Honours in the other place thought about it, but I can guess that they found it quite shocking. We have come a long way from that day to the recognition that governments are obligated to provide for the security of our older people. I will not only agree, but assert that the Old Age Security Act, the Canada Pension Plan and other forms of benefit are much better than the Government Annuities Act itself, but I regret that it is being removed completely without more substantial improvements being made in the other forms of old age retirement income.
I welcome the percentage increases that those now drawing annuity payments will receive retroactive to April 1. I welcome the fact that in respect of contracts still in existence and not yet matured the r.ate will be 7 per cent as from that same date. But I regret that there is not in this legislation a formula for escalation year by year. As for the other forms of retirement income, you know, sir, and this House knows that the battle for further improvements in all our pension plans will go right on until we win.
November 18, 1975

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the references by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to that great parliament of 1908. He spoke with such reverence and affection that I thought I may have misread history. However, I find that I have not done so. That was the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier; I believe he was in power at that time.
The hon. member spoke of that government with such affection that I thought perhaps he had been a member of parliament at that time. But I checked the parliamentary record while he was speaking and found that was not so. Sir Wilfrid Laurier has gone to his just reward, and the government of that day eventually went to its just reward and other governments came into play, including the party which is now the official opposition.
The whole history of pensions, the protection of the disadvantaged in Canada, whether one party or another has been in power has been a history of progress. While there may be comments made from time to time, partisan or otherwise, in front of or behind the curtains of this House, in respect of that progress, the men and women of that day who took those steps, regardless of the party to which they belonged, took them in the hope there would be improvement for those who were intended to be beneficiaries.
I think it is important to remember with regard to this piece of legislation that perhaps it marks the beginning of the end of an era. We must remember there was skepticism in the business community. It was an unusual idea in 1908 that there should be this kind of provision for one's old age; therefore, the private insurance companies and financial institutions, which are now the everyday common carriers of the type of protection the annuities are meant to provide, would not touch it with a ten-foot pole. However, the government of the day recognized that there was a problem.
We have progressed a considerable distance past the point where it can be said that the government is the only kind of organization that can provide adequate protection. In fact, this kind of protection against the vicissitudes of old age has reached the point at which it has become much more popular, so popular that the private carriers are deemed to be able to do this work. I think it is important because it relieves to a certain extent the government of the day from the expenditures that are necessary under a program such as this and allows it to look to other programs that are also necessary in our community.
I think it is important because there is an implicit recognition here that there is an opportunity in the private enterprise sector of our economy for that aspect of our economy to function. The government is recognizing that at least in this field they can begin to phase out in a just and equitable way the particular kinds of coverage which were intended by the government in 1908.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre passed rather lightly over the opportunities for Canadians to invest in their country through investing in annuities. But that, too, is being provided for in a different way. If investment in one's country is a criterion, I think we have to look at the Canada saving bonds program which is a
Government Annuities
form of investment in one's country and in which much more flexibility is provided for the owner of the bonds, in terms of his use of the fund during the time it is required. The necessity for this kind of program is not nearly as apparent from that point of view.
I am one who supports, as a matter of principle, the indexing of pensions and I have spoken in the House about that. We will have the opportunity to deal with the whole broad field of public service pensions when we deal with Bill C-52. There is there a form of indexing, although it is not quite in the sense that has been mentioned, in that the governor in council has the right to look at the conditions and to advance interest rates if it becomes necessary and, I suppose, to advance them dramatically. The minister has indicated that conditions have become such that the government must have this power built into the regulations. The government is saying, in effect, that they really cannot predict the conditions and that the Minister of Finance will not predict or forecast what either the growth rate or the inflation rate will be-and that is one of the terrors of our time, quite frankly, for the person who has recently purchased or will purchase a government annuity as some protection against financial insecurity in old age.
What is really happening is that the government is saying in this piece of legislation that things have become so bad and so difficult that even the experts are failing to predict what the conditions will be in the business and financial communities, with all our income controls and anti-inflation programs, for senior citizens and others. Perhaps it is an admission not just of the failure of the government but of the failure of our economic system in the scheme of things. That is why the minister has seen fit to put in place some form of index-I use that word in the broadest sense-j?y regulation.
The fear that I and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre have, quite frankly, is that the event will follow the necessity for indexing and by using this kind of system the minister has taken upon himself the considerable onus of ensuring what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said would happen, that is, that the increases in the return will match what is happening in the community to a great extent.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE RATE OF RETURN ON GOVERNMENT ANNUITY CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that we are finally getting around to the business of correcting the injustice done to those people who have been holding government annuity contracts for so many years. This bill is long overdue and I doubt that we will take much time in debating a matter that should have been settled long ago. While I realize that we cannot go back in years and grant a higher rate of interest on these annuities, we might at least have gone back to January 1 of this year and not just to April 1. This would have made up a little for what these people have lost through the great increases in interest rates that we have experienced over the past ten years.
I thought the government would have set the interest rate on these annuities at 9 per cent to 9.5 per cent, the same as the current savings bonds. I do not see any difference in collecting public money by subscription, whether you call the program an annuity or a bond issue. If government savings bonds realize a rate of interest of 9% per cent per annum, why should there not be the same rate of interest for another bond issue? Just because an issue is called by a different name does not mean it should qualify for a lower rate of interest. We should have taken the opportunity to do this last fall when the government set the new interest rates on savings bonds. At that time my party called on the government to establish the same interest rates for annuities as for savings bonds, but we had to wait a full year for that to be done.
The provisions of this bill would have been speedily passed through this House any time in the past ten years. While my colleagues and I welcome all the changes proposed in the bill, we should still like to see annuities more on a par with savings bonds. With regard to the restriction on further sales of annuity contracts, there is no likelihood of anyone opting to buy annuities, even at the new rate of interest of 7 per cent. I am pleased that the government will allow interest to accrue on annuities after the death or disappearance of the annuitant. That will at least be of some advantage to beneficiaries of annuities. However, I do not see any provision in this bill for people who are now holding annuities where the interest payments have stopped. Perhaps the government has some plan to correct this situation.
I am also pleased with the provisions which allow for more flexibility in managing the annuities, such as the provision allowing for the payment of moneys due on annuities to be paid into a registered retirement savings plan. I notice, too, that all restrictions on the changes which a beneficiary might make in an annuity contract 
have been removed, giving these annuities the same flexibility as other bond issues.
In conclusion, I should like to draw attention to clause 11 of this bill which allows for the future setting of interest rates for annuities by order in council. This should give to the government all the authority it needs to raise the rates from time to time as long as any of these annuities remain in existence. With these remarks, I hope we can receive co-operation from other parties in the House in bringing this long overdue legislation into effect. This will help those people who have put so much trust in the Canadian form of justice but who have been denied that justice in the field of saving for their old age.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can make no claim, as was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), to having a lifelong interest in this particular form of annuity. At the outset of my remarks, however, I do declare that I have an interest in this form of annuity. While absent from Canada during the war years, when one was not able to take overseas all the pay he was drawing, or when one wished to leave something behind by way of savings, I did this and my father invested in a Canadian government annuity in the expectation that the time would come when I would draw the full $100 annuity. At that time it sounded like a very valuable form of investment.
Having declared this, I do not want to be prevented from entering this debate because, as the minister knows, the announcement in the Speech from the Throne that the government was to introduce legislation amending and upgrading Canadian government annuities aroused tremendous interest across the country. I and many hon. members of this House received many letters asking when this legislation would come forward, how much the increase would be, and when it could be expected.
I therefore concur with my colleague, the hon. member for Victoria-Haliburton (Mr. Scott), that this legislation is long overdue. The 4 per cent rate is so outdated in present-day terms that I think the government was forced by the number of supplications received from its annuitants to move. I am not sure it would have moved had there not been these letters and requests. Because of the interest this matter has aroused throughout Canada, we now have this legislation before us, but we had had it for only a week.
When I first quickly read the legislation I thought I might propose an amendment or two, either with regard to the rate of interest or to the backdating of the legislation beyond April 1, 1975. I was thinking of those who had the prudence 30, 40 or 50 years ago to set aside some small savings in the expectation that they would be receiving their annuities in full form in the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s. They could not then have realized how small the annuity would be in terms of its purchasing power. In terms of savings, the amount saved in the 1940s and 1950s and put aside for-let us say $100-the $50, $20, $25 or $28 is just about the value they are now getting out of it.
On that 4 per cent there was no saving whatsoever. I had therefore thought I might try to move back the date when it would be applicable, or suggest an increase in the rate of interest. I was deterred from doing so for two very good reasons. One, of course, is that in the present circum-
November 18, 1975

stances of restraint, and having heard the figures given by the minister when he moved second reading of this bill, that for 1975-76 alone it would mean an increase of about $38 million, if my figures are correct. To suggest another year back would at least double that figure. Therefore, I refrained from taking that course.
However, I do feel that had the government acted much earlier, the increase in the back payments to bring the annuity up to its 7 per cent rate would have been easier to agree to. I am always learning about things in parliament and I have absorbed much in the course of my being in parliament for about three years. I know that in regard to a bill involving an increase in the expenditure of money or the attachment of public funds there has to be a recommendation. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre may put me straight on this, but I notice there is no recommendation in this bill. I hope the bill is not defective in this respect and that we will be able to proceed with it.
I welcome the degree of flexibility attached to this bill. Clause 3(2) accords the governor in council authority to regulate in respect of an annuity the 7 per cent rate, with 7 per cent as a floor. It will never go below 7 per cent, as I read the bill. In terms of excessive inflation, it might go above that figure but never below. That suggests, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, that those holding an annuity at 3 per cent can be assured $132 per month; at 3.5 per cent, $129; and at 4 per cent, $122. I hope the minister is nodding his head in affirmation. Those holding a 5 per cent annuity will draw $114, and those holding the 5.25 per cent, $110. Annuity holders will welcome this news.
I am not sorry to see the government no longer involved in the sale of annuities. Their sale goes back to June, 1908, when individuals bought annuities from the government. If people could have bought private annuities more easily, their private annuities would have borne rates which accommodated themselves to changing circumstances. Perhaps the rates could have been renewed every five years. Annuitants would not have been stuck with 3 per cent, 3.5 per cent or 4 per cent annuity rates. The inflexibility was written into the original act. Private companies obviously would have concluded much more flexible agreements with annuity purchasers and provided for the periodic re-examination of interest rates. I am glad that the government is no longer involved in this activity.
Nowadays a prudent saver can put aside money in many ways: he can invest in a Canadian business, buy government bonds and otherwise provide for his family's future. He can invest in his country. I am glad that opportunity is becoming more widespread. Therefore, calling this legislation long overdue, welcoming many of its features, I will not delay passage of this bill on second reading and its going to committee for further study.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE RATE OF RETURN ON GOVERNMENT ANNUITY CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to take up much time talking on this bill, although I wish to bring a few points to the minister's attention. Like most members, I have received substantial correspondence from constituents on the subject of government annuities, perpetual government bonds, etc. Many people purchased annuities and perpetual bonds before we
Government Annuities
experienced our present degree of inflation. All their complaints are similar, namely, that when they made their original investments they considered them to be good, substantial, so-called blue chip investments. Inflation was virtually non-existent and they visualized their future as being reasonably stable. Their horizon was unclouded and they bought such investments to provide for their retirement years.
When I heard that the government was to bring in legislation to increase the effective rate of interest on annuities but terminate their sale, I became concerned. The fact is, people are involved with governments and, like it or not, dealing with government is different from dealing with a private concern. The government's determination to end the sale of annuities is a glaring admission of the government's failure not only in annuities but in bonds generally. It is a failure to adapt to circumstances and the economic needs of those most in need. Primarily, of course, we are talking about senior citizens and the elderly who contributed to their country by working diligently over the years. They put away money for their retirement years but now, because of present-day conditions, they are under a great disadvantage and severely inconvenienced. That being so, it is appropriate for hon. members to raise their voices in protest and ask the government if this bill is fair and if something more could not be done to help these unfortunate people.
I realize that my suggestions involve considerable expense. Some of my colleagues suggest that the bill should be retroactive, that increased interest should date back to the original date of purchase of the annuity. Annuity holders are asking for more interest. They do not say that the effective rate should be, say, 7 per cent back to the original date of purchase, but they do say that the rate could be indexed to bring it in line with the rate paid by a reasonable investment in the years intervening between the original purchase and the present. If a fair and reasonable rate at the time of purchase was 3.5 per cent, that was the going rate for investments but it is too low now: it is now unrealistic. The government in its announcement of this bill indicated that it is ending the sale of annuities because it says there is insufficient interest in this type of investment. To me, that is an outright admission that people are losing faith in government investments.
I now take issue with some of my colleagues who say the government should get out of the annuities business. I feel that the government should play a certain limited role in the field of annuities. Certainly, it raises money by selling bonds and notes but it is under the social obligation to involve itself in a reasonably limited scheme of annuities. It should make them available primarily to lower income people who have not enough money to provide for their retirement through contracts with private companies. I, for one, am sorry to see the government leave the annuities business. I suspect it is leaving because of its unfortunate experience in that business and the serious complaints it has received:
I said at the beginning that most of us receive letters from our constituents. I have received a number. One from a constituent illustrates the plight in which many find themselves. The writer is a fine person, a widow in my constituency who has made a substantial contribution to

November 18, 1975
Government Annuities
her community, province and country. Among other things, she has worked very hard all her life. In 1954 she purchased a government annuity. She invested her savings of $12,000 through the office in Saskatoon and, I believe, made payments over three years. After she finished making her payments she reconsidered the investment. Even then she had serious reservations, and at her own expense travelled to Ottawa to see the director of the annuities branch. She asked if she could withdraw from the annuities scheme but was advised that it was a firm contract in the same way as if she had dealt with a private corporation. The government was not prepared to make any exceptions to the rule. Therefore, she was tied in, if I can term it in that way-

I will say tied "tied." You can put your own interpretation on it. She was in fact tied into the scheme and could expect no relief or exceptions to the rule if she made a petition or formal request to the government. This woman was then advised that the scheme in which she was involved was a straight annuity concept. She was told that if she did not take the option to put it into a guaranteed scheme for a period of years, in the event of her death over the next few years, there would be no residual interest on the part of her estate with respect to any of the funds she had invested in the annuities scheme. Rather, it would simply terminate and the contract would be finished.
As a result of receiving this information, this woman opted for the annuity guaranteed scheme for 20 years. That was well and good. I understand she received an effective rate of 3'/2 per cent on her investment. Another aspect of this contract which I find rather inequitable is that when this lady reached the age of 65 years, not only was she still receiving the same interest rate of 3lA per cent but by virtue of the operation of this annuity the amount that she received in old age security was deducted from the annuity. Therefore, she received something like $40 less each month than she would have received had she not been in receipt of old age security. We have spoken about the inequity of return on interest rates. However, I find it a very disturbing situation when a government plan penalizes a participant by virtue of the fact that he or she is receiving old age security payments because they have passed the age of 65.
When this matter comes before the standing committee I will be interested in hearing from the minister whether provisions of this sort contained in annuity schemes will be amended to make the scheme more equitable and to underline the concept of an annuity. It should be on the same basis as if one had an annuity with a private company. It should not be affected by the kind of payment one receives from the government as a matter of right having attained the age of 65. In addition to speaking to me, this lady has apparently spoken to the CBC ombudsman. I understand there may be some discussion of this particular problem on that program before the end of this month. I can only hope that this complaint, which was brought to the attention of the minister, had some effect in precipitating this legislation. If that is the case, I suspect Mrs.

Margaret Jenkins, a very distinguished constituent, will be happy that her complaint and petition have had this effect.
While this legislation may not go as far as one would like, it does go a certain distance toward bringing some equity to these investments as of April 1, 1975. I join with other hon. members in commending the government to the extent that they have taken action to make a more reasonable return available to participants in the annuities scheme.
In writing to me, Mrs. Jenkins pointed out that if she had purchased $12,000 worth of government bonds at that time, she would have received $540 a year, or $10,800 for 20 years until April, 1975 at which time she would have received back the $12,000. She would still have had her capital. What she has now is a guaranteed period of 20 years with her $12,000 investment. She receives something in that vicinity but she has used up the capital investment. This woman has children. She feels she has contributed to society and to her country. She saved money. Quite frankly, she does not believe she has received proper consideration. During the course of the committee proceedings I hope the minister will give serious consideration to what else might be done for people in this situation.
I am certainly in favour of restraint in government expenditures. However, there is an area of government priority that must be considered. I refer to those who are unable to take care of themselves, the disadvantaged and the elderly. These persons have a very high priority. Restraint in government spending can well take place in other areas. A rearrangement of priorities in spending would not be difficult in order to make some reasonable provision for people in the categories I have mentioned.
During the course of the committee meetings, I ask the minister to let us know whether there is any additional provision which might come within the royal recommendation, by which we can make some gesture toward persons who will receive minimum benefit from the provisions of this bill, those whose annuity contracts are coming close to termination. These are special cases. The government is regarded by citizens in somewhat different terms than private companies. I therefore ask the minister to set up within the annuities branch an administrative tribunal to look at individual cases and grant relief with respect to applications where a particular hardship or need is shown. It is all right for those who have a reasonable income to just look upon this as an investment, but many people in Canada rely extensively on this kind of investment.
It seems to me the minister would do Canadians a great service if he were to consider setting up a mechanism within the department through which applications or petitions could be made by people who are most seriously affected by inadequate interest rates over the years; they might be given an opportunity to seek relief additional to that proposed in the legislation. In conclusion, I appreciate the opportunity afforded me to take part in this debate. I have spoken for rather longer that I intended, but I had certain things I wished to say with regard to this piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to intervene briefly in this debate because I, along with others in this chamber, have received letters and telephone calls from people who have asked for the very thing which is being granted in the bill now before us.
In the past, when a great many people, now older people, purchased government annuities, they did so for two reasons. First, the 4 per cent interest rate was not unattractive when compared with the bank interest rate and the interest rate yielded by other easy investment opportunities at the time. In the second place-and this was perhaps the major reason-they felt that if any investment was gilt-edged and secure, a government annuity stood in that category since it was backed by all the resources of the country.
Then a few years ago when inflation began taking hold of the economy, their investment looked far less attractive and members began receiving letters pointing this out. Several hon. members have referred to these letters but I do not believe any have been put on record. I intend to quote one of them because it expresses in a forcible way the plight of those concerned. It is from Sydney W. Mason, R.R.l, Selkirk. He writes:
Dear Mr. Knowles:
In the sixties, the government promoted the sale of Canadian Government Annuities to provide a retirement savings plan. Many people like myself put in sums in excess of $1,000 per annum as a responsible provision to retirement. In course of time the government annuity was taken out and a monthly income established. This is administered through the Unemployment Insurance Commission ... These annuities were established at a rate of 4 per cent on the capital and since that time have been paid on that basis. As a fixed income it does not change, and I am sure in those days nobody anticipated the high inflation or the rise in interest and it seems to me the government could well pay a yearly bonus to reflect conditions today, not on the basis of 4 per cent. This was appreciated in the case of Canada savings bonds where a bonus was brought in last year, and old age pensions and welfare have been geared to inflation, but those of us who had the foresight to provide for ourselves without government support are penalized and the government is "ripping us off" by investing our capital and paying us at 4 per cent.
That, I think, is the crux of the situation, and no doubt representations of this kind are the reason Bill C-75 is before us today. Following such representations as I have quoted, I wrote to the then minister of finance, now the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) and among other things I said:
It would be reasonable to ask the government to index annuities in the same manner so that their value is not completely eroded.
I was referring to the indexing of bonds.
I draw this matter to your attention at this time because no doubt in the near future you will be introducing a new budget in the House of Commons and it would be the opportune time to take some steps to protect the income of people who have government annuities and other low paying interest bonds.
I do not by any means claim that this letter prompted the minister to take action, but no doubt letters addressed to
Government Annuities
him and representations by hon. members generally encouraged him to take the step he did. The 7 per cent interest rate is to be commended. It is a great improvement on the 4 per cent figure I have mentioned. I think, though, it might be better to index the interest rate rather than provide for its adjustment by order in council. It seems to me it would be fair to index it in accordance with the cost of living, the consumer price index, and so on. Even the 7 per cent rate is not particularly attractive when one considers the interest which can be earned on savings deposited with banks, or on savings bonds. While good, the 7 per cent rate could certainly be increased without hurting anyone.
I was interested in the proposition the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) made about the need to look at the perpetual government savings bonds which are held by large numbers of people across the country. These are a millstone around the necks of their holders, in terms of investment. The interest rate is abysmally low. This is another item about which my constituents have been making representations to me, and there is a growing need for action in this area.
In conclusion, I express the hope that agreement will be reached, as the debate closes, to go into committee of the whole. Let us get this bill through and get the money into the hands of the people concerned as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, may I say, first of all, that I regret the failure of the House leader to obtain unanimous agreement among the parties to sending this bill before a committee of the whole House after second reading. It is not always easy for members interested in particular pieces of legislation to find places on the various committees which are created. A person having an interest in Bill C-75 would find, with some surprise, that the Department of Manpower and Immigration was going to handle it as originally introduced or referred to in the House by the Minister of Finance.

It could just as well, and more expeditiously, be done in committee of the whole. Many of us had also hoped that this bill would be given third reading today. I am glad it is not the party to which I belong that has put the roadblock in the way of its speedy passage.
There are two or three comments I would like to make, and I hope the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) will be able to answer my queries in his summing up. This being one of the dwindling number of government long-term borrowings on which Canada Pension Plan rates of interest are based, that is, the rate the provinces pay the federal government for the use of Canada Pension Plan moneys, is it the position of the government that their actions concerning this bill are entirely altruistic? In other words, does the prospect of raising the interest rate with respect to the Canada Pension Plan have any bearing on the decision, and does this measure indicate that the government's other long-term securities may be subject to adjustments-the government's definition of a long-term security being that it must be of 20 or more years' duration? There are very few

November 18, 1975
Government Annuities
securities in a government portfolio, and removing a Canadian annuity fund from that portfolio is going to affect Canada Pension Plan interest rates.
I think clauses 3 and 4 leave one in a considerable fuzz about the real rate of increase in pay-out. Annuities being paid out prior to April 1 will now be increased to 7 per cent interest. This bill is, as has been said, long overdue and I am pleased to support it. I hope it will get speedy passage.
I close on a lighter note. I would ask the minister, or anybody, to explain to me the intriguing phrase in clause 8, "the purchaser has died or gone out of existence". I must confess I have been puzzling over how you go out of existence rather than die. I had no idea that there was an alternative.
