With regard to the real rate of pay-out increase, I am not sure why there is confusion there. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) was quite accurate in the figures he placed on the record, as I heard them. The $100 payment, depending on the schedule, is increased in proportion to the percentage rates at the back of the bill.
As for the expression in clause 8 "died or gone out of existence", I admit that puzzled me a bit. It is really the difference between a human and a corporation. Humans, unfortunately, die; corporations go out of existence for all sorts of reasons. There may have been a better way to put it, but that is the intent of that somewhat amusing use of language.
With regard to the proclamation date, we are only reserving the implementation of this legislation in order to have the opportunity, after receiving the authority of the House of Commons, of proceeding with a certain program of administrative measures getting them in line. This will be done as quickly as possible because we are very keen to get the cheques rolling. Hopefully, this will coincide with the availability of delivery of the cheques. I look forward to discussing the bill in more detail in committee.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
that Bill C-71, to amend the Criminal Code and to make related amendments to the Crown Liability Act, the Immigration Act and the Parole Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, first I want to thank the House leaders opposite for arranging that this bill be called at this time. I hope it will be possible to refer the bill to the
November 18, 1975

Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs after appropriate debate and to have the bill passed by this House and the other place by Christmas. I recognize, as does the government, the concern of Canadians for the whole question of prevention and detection of crime, and peace and security. This is a major concern that is surpassed possibly only by the concern of Canadians for inflation.
The government believes that Canadians have the right to enjoy a sense of safety on their streets and in their homes and cities, a right that has long been the hallmark of our country's way of life. There are many Canadians who feel insecure in this regard at this time. The policies and initiatives which the government will bring forward to the House in the months to come will tackle the issue of how Canada must respond to social and cultural changes. Initiatives will be forthcoming in a number of areas. Some, as hon. members know, such as the national attack on inflation, are already before the House. Others, such as bills which I and my colleague, the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), are working on now will be introduced shortly. They are currently in preparation and under consultation on a priority basis with the attorneys general of the provinces and others.
This bill which was introduced by my predecessor, now the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), during the month of July and introduced today for second reading is part of a series of measures which will demonstrate, I think, in a full and firm manner the government's determination to respond to the real and legitimate concerns of Canadians. I hope we can get it into the committee after appropriate debate in order to deal with both the substantive and technical amendments provided for in Bill C-71 in the precise way that committee hearings allow.
The criminal law amendments bill is one of a number that have been and will be introduced in a continuing review by the government of the Criminal Code. This ongoing reappraisal of substantive, procedural and evidentiary aspects of criminal law is necessary if criminal law is to reflect the changing attitudes of Canadians and to provide for more effective means of law enforcement against criminal activities. It also provides the means of evaluating the effectiveness of some earlier changes with a view to ascertaining whether further modifications or improvements are needed.
Increasingly, crime is taking on an international aspect and the amendments dealing with conspiracy and laundering are aimed at these particular problems. Changes in our mode of life, such as the increased use of credit cards, have made it necessary and desirable to introduce provisions dealing specifically with credit card theft, fraudulent use of credit cards and theft of telecommunications services.
The amendments that are being introduced in Bill C-71 result, in some instances, from particular problems that have been encountered and in others from a general realization that the present provisions are inadequate to meet changing conditions. These amendments are designed to remedy the problems that have been encountered or are anticipated.
Criminal Code
Many of the amendments contained in the bill are the result of representations made by the criminal law section of the Uniform Law Conference, the Canadian Bar Association, the attorneys general of the provinces, law enforcement authorities and the general public. These representations are indicative of the participatory nature of the amendment process whereby all segments of the public are involved. I will at a later date, when further amendments to the Criminal Code are introduced, be discussing both these amendments and the work of the Law Reform Commission in the whole area of criminal law reform which will be going on over the next few years.
The main objectives of the bill are fourfold. They are to update certain areas of the criminal law to reflect the changes in public attitudes; for example, provisions dealing with pinball machines and interprovincial lotteries. The second is to take account of crimes which have recently become more prevalent, such as fraudulent use of credit cards, as I have mentioned. The third is to strengthen the provisions of the Criminal Code where problems have persisted, such as bail, drinking and driving offences and cattle theft. The fourth is to modernize provisions dealing with the legal process and criminal procedure, such as rape and related sexual offences.
I want to deal, at second reading, only with a number of aspects of this series of amendments. One of the major problems facing law enforcement authorities across the country in recent years has been the inroads made into our society by organized criminals, white collar criminals or syndicated crime, as they are variously called, who are adept at using the legitimate institutions of society as a means toward illegal ends. For example, consider the case of bonds or securities stolen outside Canada's borders, then passed through various front companies to be converted into cash. At the present time, section 312 of the Criminal Code cannot be used against those proceeds of theft but only against the actual goods or moneys obtained by theft, even if it can be proven by investigation that these proceeds do indeed derive from an illegal act.
By enlarging the scope of this section of the Criminal Code, as this bill purports to do, to make it an offence knowingly to possess the fruits of criminal acts whether committed in Canada or not, we will be placing in the hands of law enforcement bodies a potent weapon against organized criminals. It will no longer be possible for Canada to be used as a laundering facility along organized crime's cash flow process.
Another provision of this bill which will greatly assist police forces in deterring the activities of organized criminals and of terrorist organizations is the proposal to make it an offence to conspire in Canada to commit an offence outside the country, or to conspire outside Canada to commit an offence within our borders. Canada should not, and will not, tolerate being used as a base from which to plan crimes. If, for example, the directors of a company incorporated in Canada conspire to fleece investors in another country, they will be liable to a charge under this section of the Criminal Code.
In the second case, this section will make it an offence to plan a crime in another country for commission in Canada. This will apply to groups who plan, for example, to commit acts of violence or terrorism within our borders, even if

November 18, 1975
Criminal Code
those acts are not considered illegal in the country in which their planning occurs. This provision could have application, although I know the House would join me in hoping that it will not, in the security measures established for the 1976 Olympic Games to be held in Montreal.
The second area of the bill I want to touch upon is that relating to rape and related sexual offences. An area of the criminal law system which has been much discussed in recent years is the procedure in cases of rape. The complaint, and it is well known, is that the trial procedures through which a rape victim must go are almost as much of an ordeal as the crime itself, and that often it appears as if it is the victim who must stand trial for having suffered the assault, rather than the accused. The amendments to the Criminal Code proposed in this bill are aimed at minimizing the embarrassment the victim must undergo, thereby increasing the number of rapes that are reported and prosecuted. They also, I think, reflect society's changing attitudes toward this crime while keeping in mind the rights of the accused.
Under the provisions of this bill it will no longer be mandatory for judges to warn juries that the victim's testimony, if not corroborated by other witnesses, is an unsafe ground upon which to convict. This provision has been seen by some as discriminatory to female victims of rape and attempted rape. The repeal of the statute requiring judges to caution juries will put an end to such discrimination.
It has also been said that the cross-examination of the victim, by counsel for the defence, on her moral character and previous sexual conduct reaches the point of harassment. Under the proposed amendments contained in this bill it will be necessary for defence counsel to show cause, in a voir dire in camera, that the evidence sought in such cross-examination is-of such sufficient importance that it would be unjust to exclude it. The proposed amendments would further allow the exclusion of the public from the trial or any of the proceedings of the case. The amendments would also require judges, when either prosecuting or defence counsel has applied for such an exclusion, to consider the application and give in writing the reasons for denying the order if the judge does not agree.
As another means of protecting the victim of rape, the judge shall prohibit publication of the identity of the complainant when requested to by the prosecutor, which often is a particular matter of concern in smaller communities. The judge will also be required to consider a change of location for the trial and give reasons in writing if he decides not to order a change in venue. These procedures are designed, as I say, to spare the complainant the embarrassment of having the circumstances of the case become known in her community. They will also serve, I believe, as further encouragement to the victims of rape to come forward and report the incident to police so that justice can take its course and so that the harassment which has been associated with many rape trials will no longer prevail.
The third area of the bill upon which I wish to touch involves clauses 47, 48 and 53 related to bail. The Bail Reform Act was passed by this House in 1972. The primary

objective of the act was to prevent an accused being unnecessarily detained in custody before trial of his case. It has become apparent that there is a need to tighten up some of the provisions where abuses which are potentially damaging to the integrity of the system of pre-trial release have arisen.
The general rule remains that when a person arrested is brought before the judge, he must be released on bail unless the Crown satisfies the judge that grounds for detention exist. Detention may be justified either on the ground that it is necessary to ensure the attendance of the accused at trial, or that it is necessary in the public interest. In certain circumstances, however, it is the accused rather than the Crown who should bear the onus of showing detention pending trial is not necessary in the public interest. The presumption of innocence is a fundamental principle of our legal system but its uncritical application to the earlier stages of law enforcement, such as pre-trial release, may give rise to unjustifiable results.
The accused, rather than the Crown, should carry the burden of showing he should be released, in three exceptional circumstances. The first of these situations occurs where an accused is awaiting trial for a previous indictable offence. There has been much publicity about persons released on bail on successive occasions while awaiting trial on as many as four or five charges. The present provisions are unlikely to discourage potential offenders and may foster an unhealthy disrespect for the criminal law. An amendment to deal with those who commit an indictable offence while on bail will shift the onus to the accused and remedy the imbalance.
Second, the person who has previously abused the liberal release provisions will now also bear the onus of showing why he should be released from custody pending trial. At the present time this is not the case. To shift the onus to the accused where he has previously contravened a release order is justified, keeping in mind the general principles of the Bail Reform Act.
Third, under the bail reform provisions, the foreign or non-resident accused is dealt with in the same way as an accused domiciled or ordinarily resident in Canada. The one expressed exception is that the judge may, on release pending trial, require a case deposit. In some cases, the deposit has been treated as a licence to abscond. It then becomes unlikely the offender will be apprehended and brought to trial. To meet this problem, the amendment shifts the onus to the non-resident accused.
At present, the second ground for detention that the Crown must establish is that the detention of the accused is necessary in the public interest or for the protection or safety of the public, having regard to all the circumstances, including any substantial likelihood that the accused will, if he is released from custody, commit a serious criminal offence involving serious harm or an interference with the administration of justice. The basic test is whether detention is necessary to the public interest. The likelihood of serious harm is only one of the factors to be considered.
The reference to serious harm may influence the court- and it is my belief it has-into giving too narrow a construction to the main test. The words "involving serious harm" are therefore deleted by these amendments. The onus on the Crown will be to establish that there is a
November 18, 1975

substantial likelihood of the commission of a criminal offence. I think those proposed changes to the Bail Act are important to correct and remedy some of the criticisms that have been made of the Bail Reform Act passed in 1972.
The next matter upon which I should like to touch is the overturning by courts on appeal of jury verdicts. As hon. members know, there has been recently a celebrated case in which an appeal court, hearing an appeal against an acquittal by a jury, imposed a guilty verdict on the accused. Under the provisions of this bill, appeal courts will no longer be empowered to reverse a verdict of acquittal. Instead, they will only be empowered to order a new trial of the accused or dismiss the appeal.
The next matter upon which I should like to touch is begging while armed, which is a matter of concern, I know, in the city I come from and in many of the large urban centres across Canada. Panhandling, or begging has become a phenomenon affecting our major urban centres over the past few years. Often the beggars are young transients, and often, too, they conspicuously wear knives while asking for money. To many people, the sight of a knife on a youth who has stopped them to ask for a hand-out is a threatening situation. The other day we listened to a member read letters from his constituents. I could show him long, thick files from constituents of mine touching on that particular situation. Amendments proposed in this bill will make it an offence under the section of the Criminal Code that deals with assault to impede or accost another person while wearing or carrying a weapon or an imitation of a weapon.
The next area I would touch upon is drinking and driving. One of the obvious major causes of violent death in Canada is the motor vehicle accident. Too often the root cause of the accident that kills or maims is the impaired or drunk driver. Amendments proposed in this bill will both stiffen the penalties for impaired driving and allow preventive police action to remove the impaired driver from the road before he can cause an accident. The penalties for impaired driving will be increased to a maximum fine of $2,000 or six months' imprisonment, or both. The minimum penalty will be $50. For a second offence, the penalty will be a minimum of 14 days imprisonment, up to a maximum of one year. For each subsequent offence, conviction will bring a minimum jail term of three months, up to a maximum of two years' imprisonment. The provisions of this bill would also empower judges to impose a conditional discharge in lieu of conviction, which would require the impaired driver to undergo curative or rehabilitative measures.
In the area of preventive policing, police would be empowered to conduct roadside screenings of drivers they have reasonable cause to suspect of having alcohol in their blood. This measure is not a substitute for the breathalyzer system but is a supplement to it. There have also been, which I will discuss in the committee, discussions in the press and with the attorneys general relating to the suspension of driving privileges by a magistrate. I have had discussions with the attorneys general about this, which I will discuss with the committee when the bill is there.
Other amendments to the Criminal Code proposed in this bill concern themselves with attacks made against diplomats and other internationally-protected persons
Criminal Code
within Canada and make it an offence to commit or threaten to commit an act of violence against the official or private premises of such a person. Following discussions with the provinces, measures are proposed to strengthen the provisions of the Criminal Code against off-track betting and to impose minimum sentences for second and subsequent convictions for bookmaking and running an illegal messenger service.
Recently, theft of telecommunication facilities has become widespread through the use of illegal black boxes which can circumvent the electronic accounting machinery used by telecommunications companies. Amendments proposed in this bill would prohibit the manufacture, possession or distribution of such devices without lawful excuse. This bill would also amend the Criminal Code to make cattle theft a separate indictable offence punishable by a maximum of ten years' imprisonment, and also establish stiff penalties for the theft of credit cards or to forge, use or deal in forged credit cards. The amendments will also allow the courts to try the offender in a credit card case in any area of their jurisdiction where he has committed such an offence.
Generally speaking, those are the measures in Bill C-71 which I have gone through quickly. As I have said, I urge that after appropriate debate in this House the bill go to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs where each of the amendments can be examined in detail and then referred back to the House. I think they reflect the continuing concern of the general public, of our law enforcement authorities and of the Government of Canada for the preservation of law and order in our society. Too often in recent days there has appeared to be an imbalance in this regard, and it is important that the interests of the public at large be safeguarded against certain individuals and groups in our society. At the same time, obviously we must ensure that the interests and rights of the individual are protected, but this protection can never be at the expense of society as a whole.
I emphasize again that this bill dealing with a series of amendments to the Criminal Code which are both substantive and technical will shortly be followed by further amendments to be introduced by the Solicitor General dealing with a large range of substantial changes to the Criminal Code which I hope can be introduced before Christmas.
I repeat my thanks to the House leaders for their cooperation in having this bill called at this time, in the hope that it can be dealt with in committee and passed by the House and Senate before Christmas so that members of the House, and especially those who are interested in criminal matters, will be free to devote their full attention to the next series of criminal law amendments which will be forthcoming shortly.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to join the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) in thanking the House leaders and others for co-operating in bringing forward this bill at this time. I want to tell the Minister of Justice that I was very pleased to receive an answer from him today during the question period, not because of the kind of answer he gave me but

November 18, 1975
Criminal Code
because I think that in principle he is on the right track. My question was in reference to-I certainly do not want to debate it at this stage-the Latta murder trial.
I asked whether a decision had been made at the department level under section 617 because it was stated in an article in the Edmonton Journal and in the Albertan that the decision had already been made. But the minister made it very clear that this is a ministerial decision and that it will be made at his level, no doubt with the guidance of his officials. I think this shows that the minister is on the right track and I wish him well in his position as the new Minister of Justice. I think it is an honour to rise to the position of the highest law officer of the land.
Ever since I entered parliament, all the ministers of justice have been excellent, both in our party and in the Liberal party. I always had the fullest co-operation of the former minister of justice and of his predecessor who was later minister of finance. I know that the committee and members of our party will receive the same co-operation from the new minister and I wish him well.
I should like to discuss briefly the amendments before us. I might say at the beginning that we are prepared to see them go to committee for study. I foresee possible amendments being proposed and some questions being asked of department officials and of the minister to determine the effect of some of the changes that are being made in this package. I think it should be made clear that this is a package which confirms what the minister said when he first took office; that is, that he would get tougher with criminals and that as a result the government will be able to do something to reduce the ever-increasing rate of crime which is not only occurring in this country but also in other nations in the western world. The minister said openly and honestly that a similar bill was before the House under another minister of justice. Except for one or two small improvements it was really a patch job that did not bring about the control of crime in any substantial way.
The present Criminal Code of Canada is, at best, a haphazard arrangement based on British precedent, historical accident and outdated mythology. Since the implementation of the code, changes have been made by amendment in order to bring the law up to date, but we have failed to scratch the surface. I thought that that was the function of the Law Reform Commission, but we seem to be as far away from that ideal as we were four or five years ago.
I should like to refer to some of the sections which I consider to be antiquated, archaic and outdated. Let us look at the code. We can trace the foundation of the Criminal Code back to the work of Sir James Stephen. His draft code of 1868, along with Burbidge's Digest, which was really an edition of Stephen's work in a Canadian context by Mr. Justice Burbidge of the Exchequer Court of Canada, became the Canadian Criminal Code in 1892 after being presented to the Parliament of Canada by the then minister of justice, Sir John Thompson. Many of the sections of the Criminal Code have not been amended since 1892, and even if they have the same direction in our jurisprudence is maintained.
As I have said previously, the development and improvement of the code over the past 75 years has largely been by

way of amendment. The desirability of proceeding in this manner has been challenged by many people, one of them being a leading Canadian authority, professor Alan Mewett who, in an article entitled "The Criminal Law, 1867-1967" which appeared in the Canadian Bar Review, stated:
The numerous amendments present a shocking indictment of the process of criminal legislation.
Later he added:
But it is not a cause for congratulation that Sir James Stephen would be quite at home with the Criminal Code of 1967.
I think that is a challenge to the minister. Although I am not being critical, I say that it is time we were able to do the job in the various departments of parliament. I know that this bill has been around for some time. In spite of the complexity of government today and of parliamentary responsibilities and duties, it is our job to get this bill before a committee. I ask you, Madam Speaker, whether the same unhappy conclusion reached by Professor Alan Mewett could not be drawn in 1975 or in 1976. Of course it could.
What, then, should we be looking for when we consider reform of the Criminal Code? The notion that crime can be placed in a single category is erroneous. Violent crime creates a climate of fear in the streets of our growing cities. Violent crime is on the increase in Canada, so that no one feels safe in the streets of our major cities, in the apartment blocks, in laundromats or even in garages. White collar crime, though important in economic terms, is much less visible than are crimes of violence.
The material cost of crimes such as petty theft, consumer fraud, violations of the Combines Investigation Act and embezzlement, dwarfs, in economic terms, all crimes of violence. It seems to me that perhaps we should philosophize for a few moments. To control violent crime and white collar crime we must have laws which are practical and acceptable to modern interpretations of life and human behaviour. That is why, when I come to the specifics of the amendments, I should like to see the code brought up to date and streamlined to modern times. These amendments should probably have been moved 10 or 20 years ago, and even then they would have made very little impact on the change in human behaviour, as far as crime in Canada is concerned.
The value of proper laws and proper law enforcement cannot be underestimated with regard to the control of crime, but I have felt for years that we must get at the breeding grounds of crime. What are those breeding grounds? Crime breeds in cesspools of injustice. Wherever there is injustice, crime will breed. It breeds in the urban slums or in the fast-growing cities of Canada. Urban poverty makes people the victims, not the masters, of their environment. A bad environment becomes the hereditary property of succeeding generations. When I travel to various areas of this city, I see children who are forced to play on concrete and cement without necessary parks which are large enough to be playgrounds. The situation is worse here than it is in Calgary. These children are brought up in conditions which foster crime.
November 18, 1975

In order to launch a major assault on crime we must attack the conditions of despair and denial of human opportunity in which crime can grow. However, crime still thrives under conditions of affluence. It seems strange to say that it is the white collar, economic crime which is eroding our system, sometimes categorized as a capitalistic system, promoting more and more controls and less freedom. Carried to a conclusion, this kind of crime against our society will lead us further down the road of controls and stateism.
In brief, police courts and prisons cannot by themselves control crime. I have never been convinced that prisons control crime. I cannot believe, in 1975 when I walk through the penitentiaries of this land and see people incarcerated in small cells, that there can ever be any real rehabilitation and reform. It may be that we live in a soft society and that we should not let them do hard work, but under certain conditions which safeguard society surely they should be permitted to do certain human endeavours-they would be not only of benefit to themselves but also a pride to society-so that they could be rehabilitated and reformed. However, under the conditions in which people live today, even on a first offence people are incarcerated. These places do not offer much hope, but, I would say, despair.
We must also deal with the underlying causes of crime, the immense and stubborn forces which pervade our environment, form our character and determine the quality of our lives. Through long-range effort in a new land of bountiful resources, we in Canada can surely conquer poverty and ignorance. We have conquered disease. Surely we can conquer discrimination, although I am not sure we have not gone too far. We should be conquering family breakdown, injustice, social tension and despair. Certainly there will be domestic despair if we have divorce laws which are too harsh. But on the other hand I see despair when in either a professional way or in my capacity of service to my country I see children with only one parent, and some of them deserted completely.
I have seen women across this land who have been deserted. They can go on welfare because of the number of children left with them and because they are without proper care centres, but they have to carry on in an environment which in the end surely does not lead to the creation of the best of citizens. And this is through no fault of the women in question. Hundreds of thousands of men have deserted their families and moved to other provinces. We have a kind of Balkan state in this country where alimony and maintenance claims cannot be enforced. These men walk away and leave their responsibilities to society.
While we must strive to uproot the cause of crime, we must put our practical minds to work in amending the various sections of the Criminal Code in such a way as to guarantee the law's respect and so that it shall not protect the rich while constituting injustice against the poor. Some say there is a law for the rich and a law for the poor, but the law is identical for all Canadians. We have gone a long way, even in my time here in this House. In addition, the provincial legislatures have gone a long way.
It is not the law which is different for Mr. Jones, who is in poverty, or for Mr. Green, who lives in affluence; it is
Criminal Code
the implementation of the law, the ability to hire the proper kind of expertise either by way of legal counsel, sociologists, psychiatrists or psychologists to help these people and to give them the same opportunity. An example of this, although not of this country, is the case of Patty Hearst. She can afford a better trial than her friends who were arrested with her because she can buy the best witnesses, the best psychiatrists, the best doctors and, I hope, the best lawyers.
Whether we like it or not, human behaviour being what it is, we only have to look at the book "A Matrix of Evidence" to determine how important it is to have highly trained and skilled people in the field of defence and in the field of representing the state when there is a prosecution. I have often felt we should have a special school for prosecutors, because many of them develop the idea that they are involved in a war. They feel that when they go to court, they have to win their case. When the Crown, which is the state, is being represented, this must be done in the fairest and most equitable way. The facts must be laid before the judge, or the judge and jury, whether they are for or against the accused. It is only for the defence to puncture the hole and to give the accused the best advantage under the law, because we must remember that when an accused sits in the prisoner's dock he has a large police force and the power of the state against him. Many times in my life I have seen very efficient counsel for the Crown, but not always the most efficient for the defence.
It is for us to bring excellence to every aspect of the administration of criminal justice, to correction, to courts and to law enforcement in every jurisdiction in Canada. Laws must be reformed. That is what we are going to do today and tomorrow. They must be repealed if enforcement is impossible, if the majority of people find them unjust and no one pretends to obey them and, above all, if no one is willing to enforce them. Surely this is the purpose of amending the Criminal Code; at least, I hope it is.
Before I discuss a few of the things with which the minister dealt, I might say that in my opinion the government has failed miserably in its fight against crime. Perhaps all governments have. According to the latest figures released by Statistics Canada, violence is up 10 per cent, about the same rate as inflation. Last year there were 545 murders in Canada, of which 450 cases were solved and 95 remain unsolved. The rate of violent crime in 1974 was up almost 6 per cent over 1973. In preparing for what I was going to say, last night I read that in the United States 19 violent crimes are committed every minute. There are 220 million people in the United States, and I would say that our ratio of crime would be identical.
Sometimes we are very complacent and point across the border or to some other country, but crime is on the march. Like all cities on the prairies, over the years Calgary has grown, but I never thought I would live to see the time when a secretary in my law firm would leave the office at around six or seven o'clock and be mugged, as they say, on the way home. A lady who has served in our firm for some 20 years was twisted around and her purse, credit cards, and so on, taken. Women on the streets are being dragged into churches and dark corners and raped. In my city and other cities housewives lock their doors as soon as their

November 18, 1975
Criminal Code
husbands leave, for fear someone will enter the house and commit rape or other violent crimes.
The amendment concerning rape as contained in clause 8, on page 7 of the bill, is technical. This amendment would abolish the requirement of a warning as to corroboration in the case where an accused is charged with rape or another sexual offence referred to in section 142 involving a female. Further, this amendment would exclude questions concerning the sexual conduct of the complainant with persons other than the accused in cases where the offence charged is rape, attempted rape, sexual intercourse with a female under 14 years of age or indecent assault on a female, unless notice of such questions has been given and the presiding judge, magistrate or justice considers them necessary after a hearing in the absence of the jury and the public. In other words, the court must use its discretion.
Let me deal with corroboration. I support this concept, although I shall be raising some questions concerning it in committee. There is a reason for our rule of corroboration. Rape is the easiest offence to charge, the hardest to defend. So, wise men and women over the years have said that when this serious crime is charged, which at one time carried the maximum penalty of life imprisonment, there must be some corroboration. Usually that corroboration is given by an indirect, third party. The law said that the complaint must be made as quickly as possible. If the woman, on arriving home after the alleged offence, complained, say to a friend, mother or husband as soon as possible after the commission of the offence, it was held that her complaint constituted a form of corroboration. The rule of corroboration has been necessary to ensure that no person will be convicted unfairly of a crime carrying the maximum penalty of life imprisonment.
Sometimes there are two accused persons involved in a rape. This brings me to my next point. Let me tell hon. members about a certain case. Some years ago it fell to my lot to defend two young fellows, 21 years old or so, who had been charged with rape. They were driving a girl home from one town in Saskatchewan to another ten miles away. As they drove, a certain discussion took place between the driver and the female and finally the other fellow left the automobile. According to the facts elicited at trial, a certain proposition was made to her and she said she would do a certain thing provided a certain birth control device was used. The driver called his friend back to the car and asked if he had a certain birth control device. The friend said he had, but would not part with it. The offence, or affair, then took place. According to the female complainant, those two fellows attacked her and only when she broke down under cross-examination at trial was there any admission of the events previously alluded to. So one can see why corroboration is necessary. That is why a judge charges a jury that it is dangerous to convict unless there is some corroboration of a material particular of the complainant's story.
As the Minister of Justice said so clearly this afternoon, defence counsel, in order to discredit the complainant, would cross-examine on her sexual experiences with other people and, in all probability, prejudice the jury with respect to the accused. Sometimes one felt the complainant was on trial, not the accused. Let there be no doubt that a prostitute can be raped. It is all a matter of consent or, as a 
famous judge said, a question of salesmanship. At any rate, the provision which will remove the right to what we call the envelope list, that is, the right to cross-examine the female on her other sexual experiences, is sound.
The right to cross-examine on character is retained, provided certain conditions are met. An application must be made, after proper notice, to the judge and the matter must be argued in the absence of the jury. Counsel can apply to the judge for permission to put questions to a female complainant about her other affairs with those she has charged with the offence because, human behaviour being what it is, it is possible that a female complainant will allege rape for a number of reasons when rape may not have taken place. Therefore, the proposed provision is good. Some ladies belonging to an association whose name escapes me would prefer the crime of rape to be called assault. They want the name of the crime changed as the very word "rape" carries with it unfortunate connotations. I suppose there is merit to calling the crime an assault as often a female person is assaulted and bodily harm done.
I am worried about the publicity given to crimes like rape. Publicity may be entirely bad. For example, two weeks ago our newspapers carried reports of a fellow in Calgary who had too much to drink and went on a hunting expedition. He went to the zoo and shot one of its fine animals. I think the Globe and Mail carried the story. Obviously, a reader imitated what he had read. Yesterday, according to reports, a fellow went out to an animal farm and shot a lion and tiger which had cost $25,000. I am not accusing the media, but it seems to me that too much prominence is given to crime. You see a certain crime reported one day and not too much later you will hear of the same crime committed by someone else in the same community. This happens right across the country. I do not think the media should carry such intimate details of crime.
We read of knives being used as weapons of submission in cases of rape. No sooner is such a crime involving a knife or a gun reported in one community than the very same kind of crime, using the same weapon, is committed either in the same community or in the area covered by the newspaper or media. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) has shown that psychotics watching violence on television may be influenced by what they see and so encouraged to commit the very same "perfect" crime they see depicted on television. Only when they are caught in real life they will find that lawyers do not whisper to judges as they do on television programs.
I suppose the community is entitled to know what goes on in its midst. I do not know the answer. I hope we can call witnesses before the committee who have studied this from the psychological and psychiatric point of view. The more you build that kind of publicity, the more you build that kind of crime. That is an answer I would like to get in committee.
I want to deal with another subject of the bill, procedures. I have read the bill very thoroughly. I told the minister at the outset what I thought. I pointed out the danger of changes in reference to rape cases. I now want to deal with some of the matters in procedure that have been
November 18, 1975

changed. My concern about changing procedures for many offences where the Crown can elect that the person either under a section-

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
I appreciate that. I am dealing with that in a general way. The minister talked about the procedures. I am talking about procedures in principle. I did not read clauses 33 or 34. I will certainly adhere to Your Honour's rule in that regard.
I point out the dangers of one procedure that was changed in many sections. I could name the sections, but I am keeping this on a very high plane. In these sections, according to the procedure people may be charged with an indictable offence or on summary conviction. It may be a matter of theft of $200, criminal negligence, or many other things. What I do not like about that kind of procedure is that the Crown, not the accused, has the right to elect whether it will be a charge on an indictable offence, which generally carries a penalty of imprisonment, or on summary conviction, which carries a penalty of a fine. In a number of sections this power is being given to the Crown. From who do they generally get their information? The police. If the police do not particularly like a person, or for some reason think that one offence is a tougher offence than another, they will recommend that it be tried as an indictable offence. In this way it permits discrimination.
After hearing the evidence, if a person is to be convicted the judge should have the discretion of deciding whether it should be an indictable offence or summary conviction because the penalties differ.
There is something else that I wish to point out. Where an offence is indictable and calls for more than five years' imprisonment rather than a summary conviction or an offence that calls for less imprisonment, you have to get the consent of the Crown in order to get a fine in lieu of imprisonment, or a suspended sentence. That was one of the hardships in the old drug sections under the Drug Act which called for five and ten years on soft drugs. In many cases where people deserve only to be fined or suspended and placed on rehabilitation, the judge had no alternative if the Crown wanted them sent to the institutions of crime that I have discussed. I think that places it on quite a high plane.
Another fundamental and basic principle to bear in mind is that in all criminal cases, as is true in all others, the onus of proof, that is to say the duty of proof, rests upon the Crown from the beginning to the end of the case. By that mean it is for the prosecution from start to finish to carry the burden of proving the case that they undertake to prove. If the Crown falls short of satisfying you as a tribunal of fact beyond reasonable doubt that all of the essential elements going to make up the crime as charged have been established, the Crown fails and, giving the accused the benefit of any doubt that arises, the accused should be acquitted.
There is one clause that goes to the matter of principle. If you are the navigator of a ship or the driver of an automobile and you become impaired or drunk, if they take a breathalyzer test and charge you, that is one thing. How-
Criminal Code
ever, under the new clause this can be done two or three hours later. What does this mean? Most people may say that this sounds reasonable, that the fellow was probably drinking when he got off the ship or out of his car. It is highly probable that after the fellow left the ship or the car he went home and had a couple of highballs. In order to prove that the state of his mind was not impaired at the time he got into an accident with a ship, and I do not know whether this applies to a vehicle, but if not it eventually will, he must show that he became impaired in the two hour interval before the breathalyzer test was taken.
The results of the breathalyzer test can go into evidence. This reverses the fundamental right of jurisprudence that a person is innocent until proven guilty. The accused must go on the stand or he will be in a sorry state. He must say that it is true that at the time he took the breathalyzer test he had so much in his blood and, therefore, would be guilty under the Criminal Code if he were in charge of either of these vehicles and became involved in an accident. He must prove that he had the highballs after he left the car or ship.
I do not like to see jurisprudence reversed. Once you start that trend, and it was done with the Income Tax Act, you will find that the onus is always on you. You are guilty until proven innocent. I look at it the other way, innocent until proven guilty. That is why I raise this matter which has come to my attention in this bill.
There is one other matter of procedure. For 20 years lawyers practising law in the bar associations of the respective provinces, the Canadian Bar, lawyers with experience in criminal law when taking an appeal from a summary conviction had to go to the district court or county court by way of trial de nova, which means a new trial before the higher court with the same or new witnesses. All lawyers know what I am talking about.
Under the code 20 years ago you had to file a notice of appeal within 15 days after conviction, do something else within 15 days, and set out reasons for appeal in the paid notice. It was a very tough procedure, much tougher than appeals for more serious crimes. We fought that procedure. Finally the ray of light hit parliament. I think it was under the former Minister of Finance. He agreed to a simple document of appeal being filed to the effect that a person wanted to appeal a summary conviction at such and such a place at such and such a time. The clerk advised the various people, and you were through with it. After fighting for 20 years I can say that there was little change. More young criminal lawyers were out of court because they made a mistake in procedure and the issue of justice was never tried.
Now what do we find? The easier procedure is being repealed, and appeals will be accordingly prescribed by the rules of court set by the provinces. Who makes the rules? The judges. I always get suspicious when handing over that function to any group of people, whether they be parliamentarians or judges. Do you think the judges are going to make those rules to create more work, or do you think they are going to make the rules simple to give the kind of justice that yourself, myself, and all members of this House want to see for the Canadian people?

November 18, 1975
Criminal Code
How many people know who makes the rules for court? They are made by judges. I would rather see the power left in the hands of the Code in a very simple form, and I hope to move an amendment on that in the committee to widen it out. It took us 20 years to get that changed, and now it is a reform for the worse. While I am dealing with that, let me deal with one other reform.
In the Code it sets out that you have to get an appeal book, and it costs you so much a folio or a page. That should be removed. The most expensive thing in an appeal is not your lawyer. If I am going to appeal a verdict in a serious case like rape or murder what is the most expensive part of the appeal?
We have legal aid-it is much better today, but it has only come in over the last short while. The thing to do is to get your 1,000 page appeal book. Some appeal courts, and I have this experience, pay one dollar a page. Now they are insisting that every case to which you refer-and you may only refer to a part of it-must be xeroxed and put in the back. If you have had anything to do with the cost of xeroxing you know it will cost 20 cents a page.
Appeal books cost thousands of dollars. There is a member here who has just finished a civil law suit. He could tell you what his appeal book cost. It cost him more than his lawyer. Thank goodness we now have legal aid because I remember that many people came before courts of appeal I appeared before, and the judge would say, "Where's the appeal book?" The poor accused would say, "I can't afford one." I've heard it said that, "If you cannot afford one you cannot come here and discuss it, because we don't know what you are charged with and we don't know what the evidence w^s."
When you start tampering, dickering, and fiddling around with costs, such as the cost of an appeal book, you would be all right with legal aid, but there are lots of places and cases where legal aid does not apply. I would like to take a hard look at that because I probably will never get another appointment in Calgary for discovery, or an appeal book as long as I live. The fees that are earned today on appeal books in many, many cases are higher than the lawyers' charges and sometimes they are pretty exorbitant.
Those are some of the things I had in mind. I am not going to deal with the question of the Morgentaler case- one of my colleagues will be doing that-except to say I am pleased with the result of a triumph of a great lawyer. I might call him by name although it breeches the ethics of this House in procedure, John Diefenbaker, the right hon. member for Prince Albert. He properly called on the minister of justice-the former one-the hon. member for Sas-katoon-Humboldt (Mr. Lang) to bring amendments in to the Criminal Code that no court of appeal should have the right to substitute its view as to a verdict of guilty or not guilty rendered by the bulwark of our freedom.
Originally the former minister of justice described his concern over the court of appeal overturning a jury verdict of acquittal as "largely hysterical". Well, I am going to be one of the hystericals tonight, because it is there, hysterics and all.

I would say this in fairness to the Supreme Court of Canada. In my opinion, for what it was worth-and this takes nothing away from the principle the right hon. member for Prince Albert brought forward-I said when the reform of abortion came in it would not work. We have abortion committees in the hospitals in Calgary. They have not got such committees in the hospitals in many places in Quebec. That is a matter of principle and a matter of conscience, and both are right in that regard. But there is the same operation going on in the City of Calgary that Morgentaler did in the Province of Quebec because they didn't have any committees. Theirs are legal, but because the others are done without a committee they are illegal. Here I would say-and I take the words from Oliver Twist-the law is an ass.
The Supreme Court of Canada doesn't make the law; we make the law. When they said on the evidence that Dr. Morgentaler was guilty the court was right because without a committee authorizing the abortion he was breaking the law. The court had the power under the statute to change the verdict. The right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert was right in that regard, to suggest bringing in that reform. And that is all I am saying about that. That is a change on which I congratulate the minister and I must congratulate the former minister because, as you so fairly said, Madam Speaker, it was a bill prepared by the former minister.
I do not intend to say much about bail, but I will say that really what they have done is to take the onus off the Crown and put it back on the accused. But the Minister of Justice cannot be blamed for that-he voted for it and so did many of us; I think I voted for it too. It was a government bill, though, and that change was made by the government, by a former minister of justice. Now all they are doing is just putting it back. That's why when we tinker-that's a good word, tinker-with little things, especially academics who sometimes have not had any experience, we don't know what we do.
I sometimes talk to police officers and I sometimes talk to judges across this nation. They tell me that you no sooner lock a fellow up for robbing a bank than he is out on the street because of the bail rules, and he is doing another bank robbery, back into jail, and out again in another week doing it again. There are thousands of cases like that across the land. And the pressure which has been brought on the Department of Justice to get that changed has been great. It is a good change. It is a matter of good principle.
I want to talk about the crime of theft for a few moments. Under this bill things are changed back to what they were 30 years ago. It used to be $50, now it is a few hundred. If it is $200 you can have a summary conviction charge laid and just be fined.
There is one thing I would like to mention to the minister for his consideration. That is fine and I agree with him. But you know what it does? It creates a haven for shop lifters. They go in and steal a hat, overshoes-a lot of things are stolen. I think when they get the second, third or fourth crime they should be tried on-and I mentioned the word a few minutes ago-an indictable offence. Those are some of the thoughts I have; it will be a haven for shop lifters. I can just see it.
November 18, 1975

I had a case dealing with that just lately. A couple of boys went in during the summer holidays and they changed the high record price to the cheap record price. So they were getting $10 records for $1.50. You know the tricks of the trade when it comes to that. I would ask the minister to take a good look at this theft section reform.
I see the Minister of Justice looking at me. I have done all this in 30 minutes and I did not think I could do it. I must congratulate myself in that regard. In summary I would say that we are going to support the amendments going to the committee. We hope that the committee-it's a good committee, Justice and Legal Affairs-will co-operate with us to get the best expertise, the best witnesses, to examine very carefully these sections and the changes to be made.
I would like to pay a compliment to the Department of Justice. In my experience, they are always very good to come with the explanations either outside the committee- and if you need help they will give it-or inside the committee. So we are prepared to support these changes with some idea that we might go for bail reform, on the question of rape as to its terminology, and we might ask them to slow down in some of these fields which are not thought out.

speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Basford that Bill C-71, to amend the Criminal Code and to make related amendments to the Crown Liability Act, the Immigration Act and the Parole Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
Criminal Code

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before launching into my remarks on Bill C-71, may I congratulate the minister on his appointment. I think he has done a fine job in different portfolios. I remember him as minister of consumer and corporate affairs where he did a pretty fair job; in the portfolio of minister of urban affairs where he attempted to do a good job; and in the portfolio of minister of national revenue where he also did a good job. He is now in the very important portfolio of Minister of Justice and I wish him well. He is very competent and a very compassionate minister, and I am sure that in these times it is important to have the confidence of members of parliament and the public that one will do a good job.
Bill C-71 is one of a number of bills that the minister is proposing to bring forth to amend the Criminal Code. As the minister said in his statement, it is very important to balance the interests of the public with protecting the interests of the individual. We live in a violent world, and I guess we are the authors of this situation. You cannot have wars, TV programs and movies showing violence, without having problems, and we do have problems.
It is necessary to look at the total framework of life and at the different ways in which we can make the necessary changes to our life at home, at school, and in the community. It is really a question of attitude. All the amendments in the world will not change those attitudes; it is the individual who must change. Until the individual changes we will have to continue making amendments to the Criminal Code to prevent the violent acts that are being performed today.
There has been a recent influx of new Canadians, and our immigration program in the future will bring many more new Canadians to Canada. New Canadians have made a great contribution to the Canadian community, but one of the things I find striking is that when new Canadians come in contact with the law they have almost a mental and physical paralysis in meeting the law. It is very important that we develop laws that they and all Canadians can understand and comply with.
In building the right attitude toward the law it is necessary to strengthen and supplement other areas of life. I am talking about developing a healthy economic community and decent housing. I think these are instrumental factors in developing respect for the law. Even though we live in an age of violence I think there is a duty upon us to change the attitudes of individuals.
We are discussing this bill this afternoon, yet there are only one or two reporters in the gallery. The gallery should be filled with reporters, and the public galleries should be filled with members of the public so they can learn what are the attitudes and ideas of the minister and of the government and the members of this House. Unfortunately we have a full house for the question period but when it comes to a piece of legislation that will directly affect the lives of all of us, both the public and reporters are absent.
Bill C-71 is one of a number of bills to amend the Criminal Code in substance, in procedure and evidence, to reflect changing attitudes and to strengthen the enforcement of the criminal law. It has four main job objectives. First, the bill updates certain areas of the criminal law to

November 18, 1975
Criminal Code
reflect changes in public attitude; second, it creates new offences for certain practices which recently have become more prevalent; third, the bill strengthens certain areas of the existing law; and fourth, it modernizes criminal procedures and evidence.
The minister, as his press release indicated, said that this bill is the work of consultation with different groups in society, namely, the criminal law section of the Uniform Law Conference, the Canadian Bar Association, the attorneys general, the law enforcement authorities and the general public, and these consultations have resulted in the changes in Bill C-71. I heard the minister say that he hopes the bill is passed in the House and in committee by Christmas. I hope he will ensure that witnesses come before the committee to give their views regarding the different changes contained in the bill. It is important that we have the police give their views regarding bail reform, that we have the attorneys general give their views regarding drinking and driving offences, and we should have certain members of the general public give their views regarding how the proposed changes will affect them.
As a simple example, many of us have received representations from humane societies across the country regarding cruelty to animals. I do not think the change made in the bill in this respect goes far enough, but I hope representatives from the humane society and other groups will be giving us their views.
I said that the legislation updates certain areas of the criminal law to reflect changes in public attitude. May I give the House a couple of examples. We are now going to make it legal to operate pinball machines provided the prize is a free game. This has been a problem that has spread across the country in many communities. Pinball machines appear to offer a very inoffensive game for people to participate in, yet those who do have been harassed by law enforcement officials because it is a criminal offence coming under the definition of slot machines. The minister has taken up the challenge and made pinball machines legal, provided the prize is a free game.
As for interprovincial lotteries, it will now be legal for lottery tickets issued by one province to be sold in another province provided the other province agrees. Again we have had difficulty regarding lottery tickets being sold in one province with the lottery being operated in another. We have to accept the changes that have taken place in this area. Personally I am not in favour of lotteries, but there seems to be a general feeling among the public that lotteries should prevail.
The second area is the creation of new offences for certain practices which have recently become prevalent. The most striking practice among the public today is the fraudulent use of credit cards, either trafficking in them or fraudulently using them. This is a credit society. I am sure many of us recall our parents operating in a cash society, never buying anything until they had the cash available. Today people buy a lot of things without cash but on credit, and they use a credit card which facilitates such purchases. However, there have been many abuses. Many people have trafficked in these credit cards and have used false credit cards. The result is that if a person loses a credit card he has real problems in trying to recover the card or in cutting off the credit in case the card is used by

some other person. Therefore I think this is a necessary move because of the change in the buying habits of the public.
The second area is the theft of communications services by electronic devices used to avoid payment of telephone charges. I had not heard of this use of electronic devices which people put on their telephones in order to circumvent a charge for a long distance call for which they are responsible. This is a sophisticated world in which we live, and these people use these sophisticated devices to avoid payment. This brings up to date the law with regard to theft of communications services.
The minister went into some detail about laundering the proceeds of crime, more especially securities converted into cash by persons or companies. We now have a great deal of white collar crime. White collar crime is committed in the laundering of the proceeds of criminal acts. The police have had great difficulty in convicting these people because of restrictions in the definition of laws. This is very necessary in view of the inflow of laundered moneys from other countries to Canada and, I am sure, the outflow of laundered moneys from Canada to other countries. It is important to curtail the activities of persons who participate in this type of nefarious scheme.
The next area is in respect of conspiracy in Canada to commit an offence outside Canada, and conspiracy outside Canada to commit an offence inside Canada. Again we have white collar crime operators who set up companies for the sole purpose of fleecing other persons in other countries. This conspiracy has been very difficult to stop because of securities legislation falling under the joint jurisdiction of federal and provincial governments. This is a step in the right direction to stop that type of fleecing by individuals engaged in these operations.
Another area that has been taken care of relates to international protection of persons such as diplomats and representatives of foreign governments who will now be protected against attacks upon their official premises or private accommodations. In this violent world we have seen these attacks on embassies, foreign diplomats and representatives, and the police and governments have been powerless to lay charges. This is a step in the right direction of developing international law under which appropriate charges can be laid when offences take place against these diplomats and their property. Those are the areas in which new charges have been created because of recent practices of individuals.
The third area is in strengthening certain existing laws, the most dramatic example of which relates to bail reform.
Back in 1972 many of us were proud of the then minister of justice for bringing forth the bail reform act because we knew of the many hardships and inconveniences being imposed on people, more especially those without money who often lingered in jail because they could not obtain bail. It is to the credit of this government and the former minister of justice that this was brought forward.
We have had the experience from 1972 to 1975 in which there have been abuses of the general principle of that reform by offenders, and this has created within the community a sense of outrage at the conduct of certain crimi-
November 18, 1975

nals. It has been difficult for many of us who supported that bill to persuade those people to understand that the principle of the bill was that an accused was entitled to bail unless the Crown could satisfy the court that grounds for detention existed. The Crown had to assure the attendance of the accused at trial, and had to convince the court that detention was necessary in the public interest. This was often a very difficult thing for the Crown to do in those circumstances, and it resulted in a bad reflection on the principle of bail reform.
It has been necessary to make a change, and this change is good because the main rule still applies, that an accused is entitled to bail in the first instance. The main exception is that the accused will not be released if he is awaiting trial for a previous conviction or if he has previously abused his bail provisions, or is a non-resident. Those are the three main exceptions to the rule. An additional change is that it is up to the individual, that is, the accused, to show why he should not be detained. This is a very important shift in onus from the Crown to the accused.
I think with these changes we will have better co-operation with the police. Many of us have suspected that the police felt the present reform act was operating to their prejudice and jeopardy, and they did not like it. It just did not have that sense of strength necessary for the enforcement of law. I hope the police are now satisfied that we are doing our best to maintain the main principle that a person is in the first instance entitled to bail, providing the Crown cannot show the necessity to detain an accused to assure his attendance at trial, or because of the public interest. I hope the police realize this and feel they have the co-operation of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and of all members of parliament in this regard. That is the main area in which the government intends to strengthen the existing law.
Another area relates to drinking and driving offences. There is not a person who has not either himself or through a friend come in contact with the law concerning drinking and driving offences. This has become so prevalent that many Canadians are acquiring criminal convictions under these sections.
It has been obvious to many of us that there are numerous difficulties in the application and procedure in respect of drinking and driving offences, more especially impaired driving, failure to provide a breath sample, and driving with a higher than .08 blood alcohol content.
The minister has attempted to standardize these offences and has increased the penalties. For a first offence the minimum penalty is to be $50 with a maximum of $2,000, six months, or both. On a second offence for impaired driving, or in respect of the other two offences, there is an absolute mandatory term of imprisonment of 14 days with a maximum of one year, and for each subsequent offence a minimum term of imprisonment of three months and a maximum of two years. One can see how important the law is in respect of these offences, and I am happy to see that the government has taken a rather serious attitude to this major problem.
Many deaths have occurred because of drinking offences.
I think it is time we were tough in this regard. These
Criminal Code
changes certainly indicate a toughness on the part of the government. I am rather happy to see that the toughness in some way is softened by the judge being given the alternative to a conviction of imposing a conditional discharge which would require that the person take curative and rehabilitative treatment in accordance with the terms of the probation order. This is an important improvement in respect of people who have an alcohol problem. The happy result of this is that if the person conforms to the terms of the probation in respect of curative or rehabilitative treatment, the conditional discharge will operate in such a way that there will be no conviction, no penalty, and no fine.
The other area concerns roadside screening. The minister comes from British Columbia, as do other members on the government side. British Columbia has had experience with regard to roadside screening of a person suspected of having consumed alcohol. We have not had that experience in Ontario or in the other provinces. This is a new departure.
In the past the police could require a breath test only when they had reasonable and probable grounds to think that the person was suffering from impaired driving. Now under the change in the law if a police officer suspects a person of having alcohol in his blood such a person must undergo a test, and refusal to do so would result in an offence. I think that is one of the preventative measures that should be taken in respect of the serious problem of drinking while driving.
The federal government has vacated the field in respect of imposing a prohibition order concerning driving and is now leaving it to the provinces to impose the suspension and prohibition. This is a result of the conflict we had concerning the operation of federal and provincial jurisdictions. I would hope agreement could be obtained between the provinces so that this would apply universally across the country. Perhaps I am wrong in this view, and the minister will straighten me out in the committee, but I believe a person could have his licence suspended in British Columbia and then move to Alberta where the question would arise whether that suspension in British Columbia is operative in the province of Alberta for the purpose of the offence the minister has left in the code, the offence of driving while disqualified.
I am not sure whether that would apply. I hope the minister would straighten out the members of the committee and the public concerning this where a person has his licence suspended in one province and then goes to live in another province. There is the question of whether that licence suspension or the prohibition would apply for purposes of a criminal offence under the code.
Then there is the matter of theft of cattle and the offence in this regard. I am sure many western members, more especially those from the prairies, will be happy to know that cattle theft will now be a separate offence under the code, with a very harsh penalty of a minimum of ten years' imprisonment. There must have been a fair amount of cattle rustling in the west. We do not have it in Toronto. We have a different type of rustling. This must be welcome news to many people in the west.
The fourth area concerns the modernization of criminal procedures. The most important area is with regard to rape and related offences. If ever there has been a subject which
