subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the dinner adjournment I was speaking about the fourth area in the bill to modernize criminal procedures and evidence. The main topic is rape and related offences. May I point out to you the amendments indicated in the bill.
First of all the requirement on a judge that he must warn the jury of the danger of convicting the accused if the complainant's evidence is not corroborated is abolished in the case of rape and related sexual offences. The second change is that cross examination on past sexual conduct by the complainant with a person other than the accused will be permitted only if reasonable notice in writing is given. The judge will then decide in the absence of the jury whether the evidence is admissible. The next change is that the judge may exclude the public in rape and related offences on the application of the accused or prosecution, and if the order is denied reasons must be given by the judge for the denial. This may be applied to part or all of the proceedings. The next amendment is that the judge may also order a prohibition on the publication of the identity of the complainant when an application is made by the Crown. The final amendment is that the judge may also change the place of trial in cases of rape and related offences when he deems it desirable.
You can judge from those changes that they are substantial. As I said prior to the adjournment for dinner, rape has become one of the most emotionally charged words in our vocabulary, and there has been a great deal of stress and

strain both on the victims and on the public with regard to this offence. I think that most members of the House and the public at large will welcome the amendments with regard to changes in rape.
I should like to direct my attention to the representations that have been made by different groups concerning the charge of rape. Representation has been made that the charge of rape should be dropped and the charge of aggravated assault should be widened to include sexual attacks. I would like to hear the minister comment on this proposed change, either in committee or when he winds up the debate.
Many people have felt that the technical difficulties with regard to the definition of rape, and also the emotional charge concerning the word, have presented difficulties. Therefore representations have been made that this word should be dropped and that a more precise definition of aggravated assault with regard to sexual attacks should be found. As I say, I think the minister should deal with this either in committee or when he winds up the debate.
The next amendment is with regard to jury verdicts. The amendment states that a court of appeal, when hearing an appeal from an acquittal by a jury, will be limited to ordering a new trial or dismissing the accused. This amendment arose out of the Morgentaler case. A great deal has been said about this case; probably a great injustice was committed as a result of what happened, so many of us welcome this change.
Another welcome amendment is the changing of the offences with regard to theft, possession, and fraud to give Crown counsel the option to proceed either by indictment or by way of summary conviction. This is most welcome because many young people between the ages of 16 and 25 acquire a criminal record and have difficulties obtaining employment. This will directly affect the Criminal Records Act because if a person has a summary conviction offence he need only wait two years before an application need be made under that act, whereas if it is an indictable offence he has to wait five years. Up to the time of this amendment the law was that theft, possession, and fraud were indictable offences, so the minister can be commended for this proposed change.
There are many other changes. There is the amendment with regard to summary conviction appeals with the abolition of the trial de novo. From my experience many lawyers always welcomed the trial de novo, especially when they lost in the lower court, because it gave them a second chance to present their cases and probably to strengthen them. However, now they are going to be confined to the record at the first trial and they may have difficulties, but we can discuss in committee the reasons the minister thought it necessary to do this.
Another change is an amendment regarding grand juries. I think we in Ontario will welcome the abolition of grand juries. I know some of the other provinces have already abolished them, but we in Ontario have not. I think this is a welcome change.
There is one more amendment I should like to discuss briefly, and that is the amendment dealing with people who are mentally ill. I am sure any person who has prac-
November 18, 1975

tised law has been in court on occasion when a mentally ill person has been charged, and the court has been helpless at times with regard to giving some treatment direction to that person. He has had to be confined, and in most cases until his trial came up, but this amendment gives him the opportunity to be remanded out of custody for observation upon consent of the prosecution and the accused. I think this will go a long way in helping these people.
All these amendments with regard to updating the law, creating new offences, strengthening the law, and modernizing the law, result in taking the drama out of court. That may be a good thing because the drama in the past has been in connection with the conviction, and it seems to me that we should shift from an emphasis on convictions to an emphasis on reformation and rehabilitation. If these amendments and other amendments direct us in that way, I think they will be welcome changes.
We in the New Democratic Party will support this legislation. We look forward to the Minister bringing forward other legislation which will strengthen the law and help individuals to take their rightful place in society.
As I said at one stage, violence is the word of the day, and anything we can to do to reduce violence is most welcome. If this bill produces some reduction in violence, if it produces a change in the attitude of people with regard to the law, and develops a respect for the law, then it will have done an excellent job. With those remarks I will close and participate further in committee.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the minister laid before us a bill to amend the Criminal Code. I would be interested to know the number of bills which were introduced in this House since the birth of this country to amend the first bill which created the Criminal Code. People in general wonder if that has become a parliamentary sport. Mr. Speaker, if it is important to have good laws that are fair and equitable for all, it is even more necessary to have those laws obeyed, and particularly to obey them personally whether one is a judge, a lawyer, a legislator or simply a citizen. One must be convinced of that truth.
Laws require changes because they are made for man. Otherwise, laws would be statutory as are all natural laws.
I will say more, Mr. Speaker, the law should be made to protect man against man, and often protect him against himself. And we dare boast we are the most intelligent beings on the planet. Seeing how some people act, free by their will, one is lead to wish God had created them like ordinary natural beings, determined them ad unum. Our will dictates our actions just as our intelligence determines their quality. And since there are no two identical beings, we need laws to make social life a bit more tolerable.
Having said this, I would like first to congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) for his new appointment-he holds one of the most important positions in this House-and for introducing Bill C-71 entitled an Act to amend the Criminal Code and to make related amendments to the Crown Liability Act, the Immigration Act and the Parole Act.
At first glance, Mr. Speaker, one would think that this bill is three-pronged. But after the Minister of Justice
Criminal Code
listed this afternoon all the revisions he intended to make to the Criminal Code, I think it is an omnibus bill. The minister says he will examine the detection of crime with public safety in mind. I think, Mr. Speaker, it is high time a minister of justice introduced major reforms to the Criminal Code to restore public confidence.
How often have we heard people say: There is no more justice nowadays. Everything is permitted in sex and other things. Today's murderer has become almost a hero who is being pampered and lives like a millionaire as guest of the state thanks to taxpayer money, of course, if not the incomes of his own victims. Today there is no such thing as robbery in business, since the real thieves have become financiers. Today there is no more usury, particularly since the government itself has taken the ceiling off the interest rate. We have only high finance and we are surprised to see organized crime rule as absolute master over our country. Mr. Speaker, I said in our country, in our province, but the province of Quebec is not the only one where organized crime flourishes. If you read the paper every day-I have a few with me-you can read titles like these: Vic Cotroni jailed in Toronto. He is the head of the Mafia. Cotroni's heir apparent target of Commission of Inquiry into Organized Crime. Disturbing aspects of Paolo Violi's everyday life. Strangely enough, all those names are repeated every day in the papers and those people go on living like nabobs. From time to time, things are made difficult for them, but it all stops there.
We are now told that the province of Quebec has appointed a Commission of Inquiry into Organized Crime to try and trace the activities of the Mafia within and without Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I think we could urge all provinces to establish their own organized crime inquiry commission. I look forward to the federal government having its own organized crime inquiry commission. I think that would be a first step towards enforcing laws which we are about to amend tonight, that it would be a start to have good commissions in order to know what is happening first and also know where the killers are and where order in society lies.
I read in a paper from Quebec that the following are discovered during inquiries, and I quote:
Drugs, extorsion, protection: headlines for the Commission of inquiry into Organized Crime. As early as next Monday the commission will initiate a public study of the Benoit project-
Do you know what the Benoit project is?
All we know about the Benoit project is that it will bring under the public eye the traditional activities of organized crime such as extorsion, protection, drug traffic and other equally unattractive activities.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, if all provinces as well as the federal government took such initiatives instead of contending that the Quebec commission is not constitutional, it would be an excellent thing. The matter is to be referred and submitted to the Supreme Court, and it would be most unfortunate if the Supreme Court should declare that commission unconstitutional. It is the only commission capable of showing the government where the problem is in order that it may propose legislation to correct it.
The minister proposes in this bill to bring in amendments concerning terrorism and the Mafia. I believe that if

Criminal Code
we are to enact good legislation we should develop an educated opinion, get date and information to find where the problem is.
If the government is serious, the basic solution would be to establish a board of inquiry similar to that now operating in the province of Quebec, to try and detect Mafia henchmen in Ottawa and Canada as a whole.
In my view, if the minister wants to do a serious job, he must first get the tools to introduce amendments he proposes to the Criminal Code.
The Canadian people want the government to enact more stringent laws if needed. The people want more stringent laws, but their main requirement is that there be respect the law on the part of legislators, those who enforce it and every citizen in general. Speaking to respect what do we do, what did we do to protect those responsible for maintaining law and order?
How often are they ridiculed and derided. This is something I am perfectly aware of, Mr. Speaker, because for 25 years I have been organizing accident investigations and other investigations of every kind. This is where I met discouraged and bewildered police officers, who had every evidence to make a fair case. They were being pushed around by judges who had other things to look after.
This is why I submit we must first protect police officers and ensure they are respected. We still have honest police officers. I have known some who, after trumped-up inquests and trumped-up judgments, were crying because they had been working for three months on serious investigations to bring about justice.
I believe that if we want to amend our civil code and enforce it properly, we shall have to develop legislation to protect those who are responsible for enforcing it.
This bill mentions drunken driving. Mr. Speaker, people are strange and governments are the same. The government favours the sale of alcohol by all available means because it is profitable and fills its coffers. The government establishes a great number of alcohol outlets, and then, when it has promoted and multiplied the outlets, it sets the police after those who have become drunk because of its own illogical actions.
If there were as many public education halls where people could be told how to act, how to fight against bad habits, if there were as many halls where people could be told why they should not drink, why they should not take alcohol, why they should not take drugs, as there are alcohol outlets, and if instead of promoting illegal outlets, the government showed people the damage done by all that trash, there would be no need for all this legislation and amendments to improve our social life.
I agree with the minister that we must bring in amendments to make the roads safer, but I have always noticed that it is when people come out of the outlets which I mentioned earlier that the police can detect more easily those who are not fit to drive, before they have to be put in jail. In the case of those who come out of the outlets promoted by the government, since this is where it gets its money, the police could simply bring them home instead of intimidating them and making them spend the night in jail. This is not being done; instead, the police patrol the roads and arrest one individual who pays for everyone else.

If the people in charge tried to be at these strategic spots, especially during the weekends, we could prevent many tragedies.
As concerns rape, we are very happy that the statement of the victim will finally be able to be used as evidence without a third witness. The old legislation was so poorly drafted that it was very difficult for a rape victim to prove that there had been a crime because the rape had to be committed in front of two other witnesses.
I think that the amendment proposed by the minister will be more equitable for the victim. The bill also refers to conditional discharge. We have noted in past years that the National Parole Board was far too lenient for notorious criminals. And under the present Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) our prisons have become boarding houses where the prisoners move at will.
I think that the rehabilitation process have not improved enough to allow such freedom. Nowadays the so-called rehabilitation takes precedence over the security of victims. I wonder whether the Solicitor General is conscious of the dangers incurred by the people when he commutes death penalties and aware that the National Parole Board frees that individual six, seven or eight months after his crime.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General hears enough protests about him to try to change his mind. As far as I can see, after having heard him in the House, he is indomitable; he cannot even see other points of view. Yet, considering how much he travels, it seems to me he should consider it. I read this in La Presse, I quote:

"Shoot them! Kill them!" That advice, those orders concerning all criminal regardless of their stature, were given, last night, to Solicitor General Warren Allmand by some hundred citizens of the municipality of Hampstead who claim to support law and order.

The Solicitor General had come from Ottawa expressly to give that conference, as guest of the Hampstead Municipal and Recreation Association. Earlier in the evening, he was calm and smiling. Standing behing the oak lectern in the elementary school gymnasium, basketball nets and gymnastic rings hanging here and there, Mr. Allmand made a speech of some thirty minutes before going on to a question period on the main concerns of his department, on its main objective, namely, he pointed out "to prevent and reduce crime so as to protect society".
Mr. Allmand described in detail, and with supporting data, the steps his department intends to take to achieve its goal. He also explained the program he intends to propose to the government before the end of the year, program aimed at preventing crime and controlling violence.
Having addressed himself to the tragic events that Canadian society has experienced in matters of crime in recent years, especially last year and this year, the Solicitor General considered the issue of capital punishment.
Let us be reminded that Mr. Allmand is fiercely opposed to capital punishment.
November 18, 1975

Did we ask Mr. AUmand for the right to destroy a human life by resorting to capital punishment? Because the execution of a murderer, as he emphasized, does not erase the crime: it destroys another life.
Shoot them, replied the citizens of Hampstead at the microphone when they were not shouting it from their places.
With arrogance and intolerance some told him that he did not know what he was talking about, that he was a moralist rather than a jurist.
One could also read the following:
LES POLICIERS VEULENT "VENGER" LEURS MORTS!
The death penalty being prescribed for police murderers, policemen realize that the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) once again tried to laugh at them and that is why today they are all against his proposals and changes. I think that should be food for thought for a solicitor general who wants at least to sound out the people's opinion and give them what they want and not what he has in mind.
Mr. Speaker, there would be many other points I should like to deal with because the minister gave us a whole list of amendments that will have to be enacted regarding criminals. We are quite happy and we expect to be happier still when these amendments are adopted by the House standing committee. Tonight I have touched only lightly on a few clauses of Bill C-71, so as to expedite its referral to the standing committee. I hope that this bill to amend the Criminal Code will promote law and order in Canada so that Canadians may live safe and free in their country.

subtopic: WRATH OF LAW AND ORDER SUPPORTERS ON ALLMAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in this debate in view of the importance of criminal law to the people of my city.
At a conference held in Vancouver, sponsored by the Police Commission of British Columbia, the increasing crime rate was discussed. Over the past two years we have had an increase in crime of approximately 13Vi per cent. These figures include crimes of violence, such as murder, assault, robbery, and rape. In the B.C. lower mainland there is a feeling, highly vocalized by the public through numerous open-line shows and in newspapers, that the government is more concerned about the welfare of offenders in society than the safety of citizens.
The federal riding of Vancouver-Kingsway alone, known as quadrant three of the four-part police divisions, is said to have the highest per capita crime rate in North America. In Vancouver east and other parts of the core area there are pockets of serious and sensational violence. These incidents accelerate anger and fear, with blame constantly turned against the government. In some areas the elderly, and women of all ages, will not use streets, parks, or stores in the city core, including such reputable stores as Eaton's and the Hudson's Bay, where they are fearful of entering parking lots or elevators since a recent series of rapes and murders occurred in daylight in those department store parking lots and elevators.
Mayor Arthur Phillips and the police commission have faced up to this through emergency public meetings, and increased the city force by 120, ready for duty by October. Plans for a proposed similar addition next year will have to be scrapped if federal support, and in particular federal activity in the area of the RCMP, is at all reduced.
Criminal Code
Illicit drug use and drug traffic alone are becoming extremely serious, not only in the lower mainland but in British Columbia in general. In our province we have at the very least 10,000 committed users of heroin, Every city, town-even villages and logging camps-has a permanent heroin user population. While Vancouver is still the major drug centre, Victoria, Nanaimo, the Upper Island, Prince George, Terrace, Kitimat, Kamloops, Vernon, Kelowna, Penticton, Trail and Nelson all have sizeable drug dependency problems, and contamination of youngsters increases yearly.
Other major factors of significance are as follows: up to 1969 the majority of heroin users were in the age group 25 to 29; in 1972 the majority age group had dropped to 20 to 24. Up to 1964 a youngster began to experiment seriously with heroin about age 18; today the age is down to 12 to 14, and a few mainliners are known to be nine and ten. In 1964 those known users under 20 years of age represented but 1.6 per cent of the total number of known users; by 1972 the percentage has risen to 10.6 per cent.
Drug seizures, although an infinitesimal portion of the total amount of illicit heroin brought into Canada, nevertheless are a frightening indicator of the drugs available to the youth of this province and, for that fact, our nation. In 1972, for example, 116 pounds of pure (80 per cent) heroin and 32,831 capsules worth at least $22 million at the uncut price were seized by the police. In 1973, 220 pounds of uncut heroin and 42,381 capsules worth at least $43,500,000 at the uncut price were seized.
Although hospital records are far from complete, the number of emergency treatment cases and hospital admissions for drug overdoses has doubled every two years since 1966.
Finally, in spite of the many pleas for action, Vancouver remains the major transit point for illicit heroin and cocaine. Far Eastern distributors have found it convenient, relatively safe, and comfortable in their dealings with Canadian distributors for trans-shipment to the United States, or as a suitable place to disguise the real point of origin of their couriers, their baggage or their commercial goods.
In speaking with Mayor Arthur Phillips, chairman of the Police Commission, he indicated that though a large number of large drug "busts" had occurred recently he would like to see the RCMP drug squad increased. This would enable the Vancouver City Police to employ men in other vital areas of crime prevention. Needless to say, the drug problem will not be solved simply by increasing the number of RCMP officers. Other measures such as drug education and the proposals contained in this bill, as well as the proposed peace and security package might assist.
The point is that even with this bill and the new crime package which is to be announced I am concerned that unless the federal government maintains its activity, particularly in the area of the RCMP, these amendments and the new crime package on peace and security will prove ineffective. I say this in view of the fact that at the present time RCMP contracts are under re-negotiation. Furthermore, I suggest the federal government seriously consider a program of financial assistance for municipal police

November 18, 1975
Criminal Code
forces, the reason being that municipal sources of revenue are limited and cannot adequately take into account inflationary pressures.
I should now like to address myself to the amendments regarding bail. Let me preface my remarks by saying I firmly believe we should not depart from the basic principles of the Bail Reform Act. There is, however, one area which deserves reconsideration.
The drug situation in Vancouver is now reaching crisis proportions. Accordingly it has been suggested to me that major traffickers, particularly those charged with conspiracy to traffic, be automatically denied bail.
At the present time I believe the law is fairly well stated as follows: in an Alberta Supreme Court case, Regina versus McClelland, the accused was charged with two counts of trafficking in heroin. The accused is 22 years old, living with his brother in Edmonton who has offered him a job pending trial. The provincial court judge ordered the accused detained; the accused sought a review of that order. At the appeal hearing the Crown opposed bail because of the seriousness of the charge, arguing that he should be denied bail in the public interest. I shall quote the decision which was reached:
I am not prepared to refuse bail simply because a person is charged with trafficking in heroin or any of the hard drugs even if he has been convicted of the same offence or a similar offence before. If he is charged with trafficking when he is out on bail or otherwise awaiting trial for a similar offence, perhaps the public interest requires him to stay in jail until his trial.
In British Columbia in an unreported decision by His Honor, Judge Meredith, in the case of Regina versus Oikle, the accused was charged on three counts for possession of heroin for the purpose of trafficking. He had a previous conviction for possession of heroin and other offences unrelated to drugs, going back to 1960. He argued that he had elected trial by judge without a jury, that it would take a year to get the trial on, and that this delay was the basis for a review of the detention order made by the provincial court judge. It was ruled that the detention order should be upheld. The report reads:
The charges suggest that-the accused might have a fairly wide field of acquaintances in the drug market; it is also significant that these charges arose after his conviction for possession. Second, there is a likelihood that if released the accused may commit offences related to narcotics. Accordingly, detention of the accused is in the public interest and for the protection or safety of the public.
From the foregoing cases it is clear that the issue being discussed is that of the public interest. In the Oikle case, public interest appears to be defined in accordance with whether the trafficker is a major one.
It is my suggestion that when the bill before us is referred to committee the committee should examine whether previous charges and previous convictions be used as criteria in defining who is a major trafficker, and that such major traffickers be denied bail.
In conclusion, I should like to congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) for the initiative shown in Bill C-71. I look forward to the peace and security package which is to be introduced later in the year by the hon. gentleman and his colleague, the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). I might add that it is gratifying to see a Minister of Justice from my own city, and also one who has been Minister of State for Urban Affairs and has a basic under-

standing of urban problems-there is of course a relationship, if not a direct one, to levels of crime.

It is a pleasure to hear from the minister, but if the penalty for doing so is to terminate the debate, since there are many others who wish to contribute, I would not want this to happen on my account. Incidentally this is the first opportunity I personally have had to extend congratulations to the minister on his appointment to this particular portfolio. I wish him the very best in his endeavours. He has a big job to do. The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) has indicated his concern at the growing incidence of crime and violence in this country, and the minister has a great task before him.
Certain provisions of Bill C-71 relate to the Bail Reform Act. While they are, as I have said, welcome,, and I think are generally acceptable, they do not necessarily answer some problems respecting bail and the granting of bail. I echo the comments made by other speakers to the effect that unfortunately what happens is that the rather more sensational types of situations get the publicity and people thereupon perceive that the whole bail system is not functioning in the way it should. For example, we hear about a person charged with the offence of murder or attempted murder who unfortunately is let out on bail under the provisions of the Bail Reform Act, and he subsequently commits another offence of violence. This gets headlines and, as a result, people feel it is not the exception but the rule.
There is no question that most members of the House are inclined to support the general concept of eliminating situations where, for example, little old ladies are incarcerated for long periods awaiting trial. We do not want to see that type of situation obtain in this country. Nevertheless we must ensure that in cases of serious crime some protection is given to the public. This is what motivated the government to propose the amendments that are being put forward in this bill.
There are some areas with which these particular amendments do not come to grips, and I should like to refer to them. It seems to me that under the present law the courts have the right to refuse bail under circumstances contemplated by the amendments. In other words, ' there is power under existing legislation, if the courts wish to exercise it, to ensure that people who may cause difficulty if released from custody will not do some damage or injury, or commit a crime. The problem has been that, for reasons that I hope to develop, the courts have not interpreted the existing provisions of the legislation to accommodate such situations.
Part of the problem is that on occasion insufficient information is made available to the courts. In this techno-
Criminal Code
logical age of computers much more attention must be given to the provision of information to prosecutors and the courts this assessment was made by those involved in the judicial process-in order to determine whether or not an application for bail should be opposed or whether the applicant concerned should be released.
There is no computerized record of people released on bail across Canada. The availability of this information is very scant. I could refer the House to a survey done by Statistics Canada, but it seems to me there is no fund of information which would allow us to assess adequately the effectiveness of the Bail Reform Act. It is therefore difficult to be categorical so far as the success of the bail provisions is concerned.
Another aspect that I do not think the bill deals with is this: under the present situation-and the bill does nothing to change it-if an accused person is granted bail there is obviously nothing to stop him absconding and failing to show up at the hearing. The rule is that an accused must report periodically to the authorities, but the tendency has developed for the police to put the onus on the courts and not to follow absconders unless they commit another offence. If they are caught and they plead guilty to the original offence, their absconding from custody is often overlooked.
This is one area in respect of which the department might possibly give some consideration with a view to determining if it would be worthwhile to develop and encourage a provincial system of exchanging information across the country covering convictions for offences that have been committed while the person was on bail. If this information could be made available to the prosecutors, with the idea of a follow-up to make sure that it is, then I think some method could be developed which would prevent individuals from pleading guilty to a second offence and avoiding, or escaping prosecution on the first offence in respect of which they were out on bail. I think this would be a worth-while endeavour and well received across the country.
These proposed bail amendments are adequate but I am concerned that they will not be applied haphazardly as were the 1972 amendments. The intent of the amendments is to reduce the range of discretion and spell out quite clearly the terms under which pre-trial release can be granted. The result sought is a narrowing of the opportunity for abuse by shifting the onus from the Crown to the accused.
In the preamble to the amendments the Minister of Justice has stated that the need has become apparent to tighten up some of the provisions where abuses which are potentially damaging to the integrity of the system of pre-trial release have arisen. The presumption of innocence, he said, is a fundamental principle of our legal system, but its uncritical application to the early stages of law enforcement, such as pre-trial release, may give rise to unjustifiable results.
The maxim of the Bail Reform Act is excellent, as pointed out by members of this Chamber, but it is one thing to support progressive legislation and another thing to make permissive the principle of that legislation.

November 18, 1975
Criminal Code
Nowhere in the original act of 1972 was there a mandate for the Crown to apply bail provisions uncritically. In fact, instructions to the courts were very specific. The accused was not to be released if the court had probable and reasonable grounds to believe that he or she would commit a new offence, repeat the same crime, fail to appear for trial, or frustrate the administration of justice. Thus it often appeared that the failure of the original act was not with its provisions but with their application by the courts. The Bail Reform Act in some instances turned into a revolving door farce in which a suspect was arrested, released, arrested, released, and so on indefinitely. The minister referred to this problem and said it had occurred within his own city.
Statistics on indictable offences committed while on bail are particularly difficult to come by because of the problem of jurisdiction and the variety of reporting systems. As I indicated earlier, there has been a survey made covering federal crime cases. This is a sampling of federal criminal cases for the period January 1, to August 1, 1973. This survey did not cover all cases but, as I understand it, was rather selective. However, some of the results are rather interesting. Some 12,698 persons were included in the survey sample, and I understand approximately 91 per cent were released either by police, by a justice or a judge at some point prior to the disposition of their cases in the courts. Of this number, according to this particular survey, about 6 per cent failed to appear in court at some time.
I am not sure how accurate these figures are because there is a lack of cross-referencing between police and court records. This makes it rather difficult to obtain a completely accurate accounting.
There are some interesting aspects of this survey which I should like to bring to the attention of the House because they do raise some interesting assessments on the way this act has been administered across the country.
In general the survey revealed that the police apparently are exercising their discretion in favour of releasing the accused. Police tend to detain certain types of offenders in custody more frequently than others. For example, only about 5 per cent of motor vehicle law offenders were held in custody, while about 75 per cent of those charged with armed robbery, and about 47 per cent of those charged with breaking and entering were held.
There are variations in the release rate between municipal and provincial police forces, and also between cities. Since this is the first survey of its kind, and there is no comparable information available for the period prior to the Bail Reform Act, it is difficult to draw firm conclusions based just on this information.
The number of persons detained in custody varied from province to province. The figures covering those cases where the police detained the accused in custody varied from New Brunswick with the very low percentage of 4.6 per cent, to Quebec where there were 34 per cent of the people retained in custody by the police. The variations in the rate may be attributable in part to provincial differences in the rate of serious crimes; that is, crimes in which the police have no authority to release the accused. However, this factor alone does not explain the differences between high custody and low custody provinces. The Quebec sample, for instance, showed only 30 per cent of its

criminal code cases, excluding traffic cases, in the more serious category, but it had 34 per cent custody rate as compared with New Brunswick figures of 16.1 per cent and 4.5 per cent respectively.
The next thing which occurred to me about this survey was that municipal police forces, with the exception of those in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, are much more likely to keep an accused in custody than are provincial police forces, including the RCMP. Municipal police forces imposed custody in 36.7 per cent of the criminal code cases handled by them while the comparable figure for provincial police was 15.9 per cent.
The study showed that the police tend to detain certain types of offenders in custody much more than others. For example, 26.3 per cent of persons charged with offences under the Criminal Code, other than motor vehicle and drug offences, were held in custody by the police, with those charged with armed robbery being 75.8 per cent, breaking and entering, 46.8 per cent, and theft over $200
41.8	per cent. Persons charged with drug offences other than simple possession also had a high rate of detention in custody, some 57.8 per cent. On the other hand police released all but 5.1 per cent of motor vehicle law offenders.
A point I want to mention is that the survey revealed major differences in the methods of release employed by police across Canada. The appearance notice, used nationally in 32.2 per cent of all cases, was used in 67.3 per cent of the cases in Saskatchewan, but in only 11.8 per cent of the cases in Quebec. The promise to appear, used nationally in
14.8	per cent of all cases, was used in 39.9 per cent of the cases in Prince Edward Island, but only in 2.4 per cent of the cases in Quebec. The summons was used in 26.3 per cent of all the cases, but its use was much more frequent in the provinces east of Manitoba than in the western provinces or the Territories.
Finally, in half the cases sampled the case was disposed of at the first court appearance. In the remaining 6,284 cases, 1,433 persons were in police custody. Out of those in custody, 1,086 were released upon application to a justice, half of them upon a simple undertaking to appear at trial without any terms or conditions being imposed. Of the persons sampled in the survey, 91 per cent were released either by the police, a justice or a judge at some point prior to the disposition of their cases.
It should be noted that of the 1,149 persons who were not released at all prior to the disposition of their cases, approximately 60 per cent had their cases concluded at their first court appearance, hence the question of release by the courts did not arise.
These statistics raise in my mind the question of the basis upon which the department makes its assessment in respect of amendments concerning bail. It seems to me some consideration should be given to having a much more thorough basis upon which to determine the necessity for amending provisions. Much more should be done in this regard than presently is the case. In addition it would seem to me there is not necessarily uniformity across the country concerning the application of the legislation. I do not say that uniformity is in itself a virtue.
November 18, 1975

However, it would seem there may be cause for the department to think in terms of an educational program in respect of members of the judiciary, the people involved in prosecutions, in order that the spirit of the law may be more clearly understood and so that the procedures would be carried out more thoroughly with a view to obtaining some sort of co-ordination between prosecuting attorneys and the courts. I think this would be worthwhile.
I am sure no one would suggest we should tell the judges how to conduct their courts because in each case they must look at the circumstances. However, I think we must do two things. First, we must provide the people involved with the necessary information, and second encourage, as I mentioned before, the concept of computerization of information and availability of information so far as the prosecutors are concerned, so that in each case they will be able to deal with the matter as effectively as possible and protect the public interest in cases where this is appropriate.
Having made those points I reiterate the fact that it is neither desirable nor feasible to keep a person in jail for a petty offence. Generally there is a backlog of cases in each of the provinces today and therefore trials often are not held for some time after the charge is laid or apprehension has taken place. I think this is another area in respect of which everyone would agree some assistance must be given to the courts and some thought given to improving the efficiency of our courts so that they will be able to deal with the cases expeditiously. If these new amendments are to function properly, the accused will have to do more than assure the court through a promise to behave.
I should like to make some suggestions to the minister concerning further provisions to which consideration might be given. Perhaps we will have to look at the question of bail in respect of a person charged with a serious crime such as murder, or crimes involving the use of a firearm. We could look at the possibility of increasing the penalty and possibly the amount of bail, depending on the severity of the crime committed. It seems to me that an amount of $2,000 with regard to bail for a person on a charge of murder is not a very large amount. I think we should be giving some attention to the question of more serious crimes and our attitude toward bail in these cases. We may want to have a more periodic re-assessment in respect of the person on bail relating to more serious crimes.
I realize that an increase in the amount of bail works against the interests of those people who do not have money, but there are alternatives which might be canvassed, and possibly during the course of our consideration of this legislation before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs the minister might respond to this and give us some idea of some of the things that are being considered by the Department of Justice, as well as some of the long-range plans and suggestions the department may have so that we can develop the best possible legislation in the interest of everyone in Canada.

Madam
Speaker, I rise to make a few brief remarks on this very important bill, C-71, which would amend the Criminal Code in several respects which I consider to be very important.
Criminal Code
Since this is the first opportunity I have had, I should like to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on the appointment of the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford). He is a colleague of mine from the province of British Columbia. This appointment has been warmly received and it comes at one of the most difficult times we have had in our history so far as justice is concerned. The incidence of crime is serious all over the country. It is particularly serious in the city of Vancouver where the present minister resides. I am very pleased with the remarks he made in his debut as minister. I think the orientation he has to deal with crime in whatever form is the right one.
My brief remarks tonight will be related to the section of the bill dealing with cattle rustling. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) referred to cattle rustling in his remarks. I believe he said there is not any cattle rustling in the city of Toronto. I would not think there would be, but I want to assure members of this House that the question of cattle rustling is a serious problem in this country, and has been for a number of years.
Over the past few years since I have been a member of parliament I have received a number of very serious representations from various groups, not only in the province of British Columbia but in other parts of the country. I have received representations from the B.C. Cattlemen's Association, from the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, and from the smaller associations in various parts of my riding.
I have received suggestions to the effect that the fines are too light and that the Criminal Code is weak and does not address itself to the very serious problem of cattle rustling in a proper manner. This is the reason why I am pleased to note that now there is to be a special section in the Criminal Code to deal with this problem.
The problem was so serious, and I received so many representations from various places, that I introduced a private members' bill dealing with it during the last two parliaments. The bill in this particular parliament is C-337. I am glad it will no longer be necessary for me to press on with this particular bill.
My bill would have achieved a couple of things. It would have provided that every person who commits theft of cattle is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable (a) to imprisonment for ten years where the value of the cattle exceeds $50, or (b) to imprisonment for two years where the value of the cattle does not exceed $50, provided that a minimum sentence in either case shall be imprisonment for one year. This is a pretty tough measure. The thing that cattlemen want in particular is to make sure there is a minimum sentence.
I know that judges in the country do not like to have their hands tied by minimum sentences, so I can see why the Minister of Justice did not accept this particular amendment. But I want to say that the amendment which the minister brought in is acceptable to the cattlemen. It provides that everyone who commits theft of cattle is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for ten years. This is a considerable improvement,

Criminal Code
and it addresses itself to the seriousness of the problem of cattle rustling.
Under the present law, theft of cattle is dealt with under a general theft provision. If the value of the property is over $200, it is an indictable offence subject to a maximum of ten years imprisonment. Where the value of stolen goods is less than $200, the maximum improvement is two years. Again I want to thank the previous minister of justice and the present Minister of Justice for responding to the wishes of the cattlemen by bringing in this amendment to the Criminal Code. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight I will reserve my remarks to the principles of the bill relating to the proposed changes in the Criminal Code on drinking and driving offences. I have some other remarks on other matters of a detailed nature which I will leave until we go into committee on this bill.
The amendments to our drinking and driving legislation are essentially a good beginning. However, I am fearful that if the new provisions pass as they stand now, their coming into force may be delayed or phased in as facilities needed to implement them are developed in areas where they do not exist now or where they are not yet adequate.
The amendment to section 234 of the Criminal Code allows the judge to impose a conditional discharge on a person charged with a drinking and driving offence. This means that the judge may require that rehabilitative measures are taken respecting the convicted person's consumption of alcohol or drugs in accordance with the terms of his order. In other words, while such a person is taking treatment for alcoholism and abstaining from its use in accordance with the judge's order, no penalty of fine or imprisonment is imposed. If he ceases to obey the order, the penalty is reinstated. In the case of such a conditional discharge, however, there is no record of criminal conviction and no penalty.
If my memory serves me correctly, this follows pretty well the recommendations of the Canadian Barristers' Association. I find that this is an excellent provision, one that goes to the root of the problem of our drunken drivers because it attempts to effect a cure. I think that it breaks new ground in our jurisprudence and, in my opinion, it is the type of thing we should be looking at more often. I commend the minister for bringing in this provision. I think it is a constructive one and it deserves the support of all members of the House.
I have two suggestions to make to the minister. There is a shortcoming in this procedure that comes in mind. If in fact the convicted person receives a conditional discharge and moves to another area where he commits a similar offence, the fact of his former conviction being erased by operation of law may not be known to the court or authorities in the new jurisdiction. This possible shortcoming can be overcome by a simple amendment clarifying the intention of parliament in this regard, and I commend such an amendment to the minister's consideration.
The rehabilitation facilities available to persons qualifying for such a conditional discharge vary from very poor or non-existent in some jurisdictions, to excellent in areas such as the Donwood facility in Toronto. This means that

all Canadians do not have an equal opportunity to avail themselves of rehabilitative facilities, and if everyone is to be equal before the law the full implementation of this section will have to be preceded by some very serious and far reaching discussion between Ottawa and the provinces.
The provinces too will have to give consideration to amending their laws dealing with the suspension of licenses. The necessity for a conviction now forms the basis for the suspension of a license by a province. A conditional discharge carries no record of criminal conviction and thus provincial legislation, if left as it is, would not be applied in these cases.
Another feature of the amendments before parliament is the provision of the roadside screening process. At present under the Criminal Code-as differentiated from provincial legislation-a peace officer can require a breath sample only if he has reasonable and probable grounds to believe that the driver is impaired. This new section, which is clause 15 in the amending bill, gives the police the right to conduct roadside screening tests where an officer has reasonable cause to suspect a driver of having alcohol in his blood. In many areas of Canada the implementation of this section too will have to be delayed until provinces train personnel and obtain the necessary equipment. The purpose of this amendment is to reduce the hazard that impaired drivers present to others and to themselves.
The amendment will certainly be a great inconvenience to a large number of people and will increase the cost of police operations, but it will also reduce many road hazards and accidents, and provide greater public safety on our highways. To many people an impaired driving charge is just as serious as armed robbery.
The strict application of this amendment will stop a few impaired drivers, but we should bear in mind that no piece of legislation will eliminate them altogether. Educating the public concerning drunk driving laws and the potential dangerousness of an impaired driver is imperative if we are to reduce the number of persons committing this offence.
Penalties are often inconsistent and based on the severity of the situation. A large number of those who appear in court on a Monday morning are charged with impaired driving, but the penalties imposed in different jurisdictions of Canada vary, and so do the programs for prevention and rehabilitation.
The new amendments before parliament will provide much stiffer penalties for those who are convicted of operating motor vehicles on our highways in a drunken or impaired condition. While the proposed legislation deals more efficiently with the detection and punishment of drinking and driving offences, it leaves one significant omission, and I would be most grateful if the minister would take this up with his provincial counterparts.
There is no mention whatsoever of any responsibility being placed on those who sell alcoholic beverages for a profit. With the inception of criminality being at the stage when a person consumes the alcoholic beverage, it surely must be incumbent on those who make a profit from its sale to provide some means of testing on the premises where the consumption takes place, so that the patron who is just a few minutes away from a serious criminal charge
November 18, 1975

can save himself from a criminal record, and save other people from his becoming a menace on the highway by taking a simple test before leaving a bar, beer parlour, or lounge in an impaired condition and sitting behind the driver's wheel of a car where he becomes a menace to himself and everyone else.
Under the new penalties being imposed, there is a substantial increase. For the first offence the fine limit is increased from $500 to $2,000, and the prison term is doubled from three months to six. For a second offence, imprisonment is provided for not more than one year, where it is now limited to three months, and the minimum term of fourteen days remains the same. For each subsequent offence imprisonment for not more than one year is increased to two years, and the minimum term of three months remains the same. Amendments to the Criminal Code will provide these same penalties for failure or refusal to provide a breath sample, and for driving with more than 80 milligrams of alcohol in the blood. Whereas sections 235 and 236, the breathalyzer section and the high alcoholic blood count section, now provide only for summary conviction offences, the proposed amendments change the import of the code and create duplicate indictable offences.
Normally an indictable offence means that a person is entitled to elect to be tried by a jury. It also makes a serious record and has implications with respect to passports, crossing borders, pardons, fingerprinting and other matters. In addition to creating a new offence for the breathalyzer related sections, the new changes have the same penalties, whether the offences are treated as summary convictions or indictable offences. This is the same situation which now exists in section 234, driving while ability to drive is impaired. This technique has been criticized by the Canadian Bar Association.
Without question the government has in these amendments shown its intention to deal more severely with these offenders. I sincerely hope some of the suggestions I have made will help the minister in his new task.
While I have the opportunity, I should like to congratulate the minister on assuming his new portfolio and to wish him the very best of good fortune.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as many other speakers in this debate have done, I should like to start out by extending my congratulations to the minister on his appointment to his high office. He has very many distinguished predecessors, and I am sure he will add further distinction to the long line of ministers of justice in Canada. I fully expect that he will exhibit firmness to ensure that crime is restrained, and fairness to ensure that it is administered with justice and humanity.
There can be no doubt that Canadians, like people in many other countries, are deeply disturbed by acts of senseless horror and violence. A general atmosphere of fear, and indeed, in some places of hysteria, exists at the present time, and this bill represents a step forward, or perhaps a few steps forward, but I am sure the minister would be the first to acknowledge that it leaves an awful lot to be done.
Criminal Code
The minister in opening, and other speakers later, have put forward the main features of the bill. I will not try to repeat that. I just want to deal with some of those features. I approve, and I think the House generally approved, of the Bail Reform Act. That was legislation to try to bring about an element of justice in order to ensure that people without substantial means could get their freedom pending trial, rather than leaving the opportunity of bail to those who happened to be wealthier and able to put up the bail required. It therefore had excellent purposes, but in my view the administration of the Bail Reform Act has been woefully weak, and public indignation has been aroused by some incidents. This legislation is a small improvement, and of that no one can complain.
The onus has shifted, particularly in cases where someone is awaiting trial for a previous indictable offence. One indeed wonders how a person who is awaiting trial for a previous serious offence would ever be able to get bail. I wonder whether the machinery of acquainting the bail judge or magistrate with the facts which would make the granting of bail unlikely is adequate.
Are there adequate means for gathering the evidence of previous criminal offences in other jurisdictions before bail is granted? I doubt very much whether there are at the present time, and I hope that with his provincial colleagues the minister will look carefully into that aspect of the matter to find out whether there could not be a more adequate system of getting the facts to the judges and magistrates responsible for granting bail under the act. I think there would be many fewer cases of people being let out on bail who should never be let out, and then committing more crimes, if there were a more adequate system.
I should like to touch on the drunken driving provisions. I welcome them. I think the amendments proposed are excellent. Screening tests by the roadside and the requiring of breath sampling are a necessary protective action for society. There are few hon. members in this House who are unaware of the multiple tragedies caused by drunken drivers. It is absolutely necessary that this wholesale slaughter be slowed down, if it cannot be stopped. I cannot see that to require a person to accept a breathalyzer test is a serious infringement of his rights. It seems to me that it is merely something to help protect society as a whole.
I am glad that the more severe provisions in this field have been tempered by a recognition that even the drunken driver is a human being, and that the convicting judge or magistrate is given the opportunity to grant a conditional discharge requiring that the convicted person accept conditions for curative and rehabilitative measures. There are some people to whom this disease is so serious that they can be convicted and before long be doing the very same thing they did previously.
I particularly welcome what seems to me to be a return to the sound principle that in criminal matters, at least, an acquittal by a jury should be given full force and should stand. It should not normally be interfered with by an appellate court. I think that is right. It is part of our history. The jury system was there giving juries sole jurisdiction to determine the guilt or innocence of people accused of crimes. I think the sole jurisdiction of a jury arose in the days of the industrial revolution where the English courts were sometimes used in cases of industrial
9224

November 18, 1975
Criminal Code
strife, alleged sedition, and political matters of that sort. The English courts were used to overturn the verdicts of juries and as instruments of tyranny.
People like the famous Lord Erskine eloquently framed the jury into a potent weapon for assuring the freedom and liberty of the subject, and I must say that I hope when this bill is passed some attention will be paid to the case of an individual who has twice been acquitted in this country by a jury and, as I understand it, is still in detention.
Another feature of this legislation is to be welcomed, and that deals with its international scope. Crime has developed an international scope. We live in an age of terrorism, and hi-jacking is reported in all parts of the world. We live in an age when the diplomat, the representative from a foreign country, is not secure, but is pursued to his garden or his office, threatened, and sometimes seriously injured. This situation is helping to destroy the whole international order. The time has come for the whole international order to take much more effective steps to put an end to this particular menace. We must, by international co-operation, take firm action to end this scourge on mankind.
This bill does not contain any adequate and fair gun control provision, which the minister has promised but not yet produced. The minister having been in his present position for a short time only, it would be unfair and ungenerous to blame him. But I suggest, considering the recent tragedies which have occurred in this country involving the use of firearms, that their control should be given high priority and not mixed with other legislation. Let the minister introduce control legislation quickly and put it into effect.
I commend the minister for this legislation, nearly all of which is worth while and deserves support. Nevertheless, I hope he will speed the pace of criminal law reform, which is urgently needed. In my judgment many sections of the Criminal Code need amending. Many, like the insanity section, are obsolete. Others are inadequate and antiquated. We have begun making improvements but have a long way to go. I wish the minister well in his task, and I say that we urgently need speedy reform of our criminal law.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this evening I wish to speak on a particular topic which comes within the scope of Bill C-71. Other members have spoken about other topics; with your approval I shall speak on something of great concern to sociologists and lawyers. Probably this is one of the most delicate and controversial subjects involving our criminal jurisprudence.
When we examine our rape laws, nearly every myth about women in modern society is encountered. What is particularly alarming is the great gap between society's changes in values and behaviour and similar changes in our laws. Before the early awakening of an enlightened society, a woman was considered a chattel or mere possession, and any violation of her was measured as a decrease in her value. In medieval law, rape was defined as "capturing or carrying away by force, and it may be applied to things as well as to women." Indeed, rape from the earliest times was looked on as offence against property. This type of attitude dies hard, if at all. Many believe that if a
woman is a sexual person, then she cannot be raped. Thus the woman is at fault, somehow "she provoked the attack." Such ideas are not easily disproven and are often absorbed by women themselves. A rape victim then begins to wonder whether if in fact she did not cause the attack.
Although these myths are rapidly disappearing, other equally outmoded ideas still surround the concept of rape. The most evident is the distinction between "good women" and "bad women." Often when an accused is charged with rape or a related offence, counsel cross-examines the complainant-to the point which some people regard as harassment-on her past conduct and general character. This type of questioning has been allowed as relevant to the issue of consent, and often it is used to attack credibility. Some contend it leads to the appearance that the victim is on trial.
The character of the accused, on the other hand, has not regularly been in issue, unless he puts it in issue. The prosecution is not permitted to question an accused about his character, unless be becomes a witness in his own defence and tries to present evidence of his good character, or other witnesses testify as to his upright character. Neither is the prosecution allowed to question the accused about his previous criminal activities. Therefore it has been quite possible that the previous convictions of the accused for rape would never be divulged in the course of his trial. This is in contrast to the severe cross-examination of the complainant as to her previous moral conduct.
In other criminal trials cross-examination such as this is not permitted. Under the new amendments, evidence of the victim's sexual conduct with a person other than the accused will be permitted only if reasonable notice in writing is given to the prosecution. The judge will then decide, in a hearing held in the absence of the jury, whether such evidence is necessary for a just determination of the case. The judge may permit cross-examination if these matters are particularly relevant. But it would appear that if this amendment becomes law, cases where such crossexamination is allowed will be very rare indeed.
Under the present code section 142 requires the trial judge to warn the jury of the danger of convicting the accused if the complainant's testimony is not corroborated. Under the new amendments the direction is abolished for all offences listed in that section, including rape, attempted rape, intercourse with a girl under 14, and indecent assault. This deletion of the warning is not to mean that a more lax standard of proof is to be applied than in other criminal offences; it simply applies the same standard of proof, that is, proof beyond a reasonable doubt. These amendments seem simply to place women on the same footing as men, and place rape in the same category as any other serious criminal charge, which is a step in the right direction.
Amendments to section 442 provide that where the accused is charged with rape, attempted rape, indecent assault, etc., the judge must consider excluding the public when an application is made for such exclusion by the accused or the prosecution. If the order is denied, reasons must now be given. An additional amendment extends the protection to any proceedings rather than restricting it to the trial itself. The order may be made for all or part of the

November 18, 1975

proceedings, and the judge may exclude all or part of the public. Again I suggest that is a step in the right direction.
There has been one noteworthy Canadian study on rape. This was a Toronto study done by Debra Lewis for a Master's dissertation in 1974. In it rape was shown to be a nocturnal crime that seldom occurs in a public area. The typical location in the Toronto study was the offender's residence, followed by a vehicle. Victims fell into the 14 to 19, and 20 to 24 age group, and were from lower social economic occupational categories. Nearly 70 per cent of the victims were single. Referring to the offender, data on arrested offenders was used and applied therefore to only 32 cases. Over 40 per cent of the offenders were over 30 years of age; 75 per cent were white and they were from lower social economic groups. In 60 per cent of the cases in the Toronto study the victim and the offender were at least acquaintances.
Rape seems to be the most unreported of all crimes, and the number of offences that are reported compared to the number in which suspects are arrested and brought to trial is lower than the rate for any other crime against a person. It seems obvious that the reason is the extremely difficult position our present jurisprudence places the complainant in when she seeks to obtain justice for the indignities inflicted upon her.
The changing public attitude toward rape and the determination to mount a real attack on the incidence of rape have been largely responsible for the government's decision to introduce the amendments contained in Bill C-71. There are, however, several very obvious amendments that have not been introduced regarding sexual offences. Use of the words "of previously chaste character" appear four times in Criminal Code sections relating to sexual offences. Among these offences are sexual intercourse with a female employee, seduction of female passengers on vessels, and even the seduction of a female between the ages of 16 and 18 years. Along with the amendments to the cross-examination and corroboration principles, these words should have also been wiped out. This again brings the character of the victim into question, and bases the crime on the prior goodness of the victim.
The Minister of Justice's (Mr. Basford) amendments have scratched the surface of the rape issue. Further intensive studies must be conducted on such aspects as the psychological, physical, and biological results of rape and related offences, before additional amendments and recommendations can seriously be put forward.
The Law Reform Commission has entered into a contract with the Clarke Institute of Psychiatry to complete a series of studies related to sexual offences. The purpose is to evaluate the effectiveness of existing definitions of sex crimes and to recommend new definitions and systems of classification. This project began in May of 1972 and is not yet completed. Let us hope that when it is completed the Law Reform Commission will be more realistic in its recommendations than in some of the lenient philosophical utterings we have heard from this expensive commission in the past. In the meantime, are women of "previously unchaste character" to be denied equality in our criminal laws?
Criminal Code
I suggest it might be more realistic, and this is something for the minister to consider, to treat the offence called rape as a form of aggravated assault. It would remove a lot of the stigma and emotion presently associated with this very ugly word from the emotional and other associations it invariably brings forward in a court of law. I commend the minister for the type of approach he is now using. I hope he will not let the matter rest where it is, but will bring forward other amendments to look at the situation of the law in changing sociological and economic conditions. I see it is approaching ten o'clock. I will confine my remarks to what I have said at this time.

speechtext:
Thank you, Madam Speaker, for your patience. Unfortunately I was in a committee of this House, and it took me a few minutes to get from the West Block to this building.
I listened with interest this afternoon to some of the comments of the minister when he was referring to the various amendments to the Criminal Code. While it is tempting to deal with all of them because they are all of significance to this House and the country, there is one in particular I will deal with because it is crucial with respect to the present situation in terms of an epidemic in this country today. I refer to the situation with respect to the

November 18, 1975
Criminal Code
offences that are committed by those who drink and drive. I have long believed that we have here a situation which has reached epidemic proportions.
As the minister and members on all sides of this House are well aware, each year we incur millions, indeed I think it would be fair to say hundreds of millions of dollars of expenses through hospital costs, insurance costs, and the enormous personal costs as a result of those who believe it is possible to drink to excess, get behind the wheel of a car, and threaten not only their own lives and those of the passengers with them but also other innocent victims using the same and who have the misfortune to come into contact with these vehicles that are essentially out of control.
I will speak a bit more specifically about this tomorrow when I have more opportunity, but I have in recent months attempted to put into effect a series of recommendations with regard to the particular situation in Prince Edward Island. I am not sure whether my office has sent the minister a copy of the lengthy report and study we have done with regard to drinking and driving offences in Prince Edward Island.
While I know Prince Edward Island is not unique in this, we have had a very unhappy history where more than 50 per cent of the accidents that have been caused in Prince Edward Island, and we have a very high accident rate on a per capita basis, have been caused by those who have been drinking and driving at the same time.
The steps that the minister is attempting to take through this amendment to the Criminal Code will be of some assistance. I hope that it is not the sum and substance of what we, as legislators, are able to do either in a federal or provincial sense. I know that much of the implementation of the recommendations that are being brought forward will remain in the hands of those who serve in provincial offices of responsibility. I believe as well that the law in some ways acts as only a final determining factor, and really only finally in a negative sense.
Increasingly we must address ourselves to programs of education and rehabilitation which will be required if we are to deal effectively with this program. The fact, however, is that we have gradually grown into a situation of such epidemic proportions that it is very tempting to believe there is little or nothing that can be done to change the direction and increase of the present situation. I believe that not to be the case.
Certain provinces, and I think of the province of Alberta in particular, have introduced some innovative and helpful programs with respect to rehabilitation. Rehabilitation is an aspect that has to be seriously considered, looking at the number of repeat offences that have taken place with respect to those who have been arrested, charged, and subsequently convicted.
I will not delay the House any longer on this matter this evening. I will merely call it ten o'clock, and hope to proceed more specifically on this aspect of the bill the minister has brought before us.
