subtopic: URBAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST CENTRAL MORTGAGE NOT BUY ASHBURN GOLF COURSE IN HALIFAX
URBAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST CENTRAL MORTGAGE NOT BUY ASHBURN GOLF COURSE IN HALIFAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, like a well polished emerald, the Ashburn Golf Course sits on a hill on one of the sides of the great city of Halifax.
The other day I asked the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) not to permit himself to become an urban vandal by trying to procure the land there for use in a housing development. I did that because Ashburn is a very large part of the gracious living for the metropolitan area of Halifax, and because it opens its doors and the course to all comers. It is not restricted. Indeed, if it were, I would not be arguing this cause in any way in this chamber.
Years ago the developers of Halifax, men of the nature of Mr. McCurdy and Mr. Piercey, and I refer back to the thirties, looked upon Ashburn as a possible source of development. The golfers, notably scared that they would lose this magnificent course, put together a special legal arrangement.
The Halifax Golf and Country Club is owned by a number of people who have banded together in a voting trust to keep this operation as a golf club. I am indebted to Major H. E. Crowell, Chancellor of Acadia University, an octogenarian who shoots his age sometimes on this course, for the information I am now giving to the House. A Halifax lawyer, Mr. F. M. Covert, put together the voting trust. That was about 40 years ago. Since then Ashburn has withstood the assaults of the developers. It helps make the city of Halifax a very pleasant place.
There are other cities within whose limits golf courses are situated. Not all cities have them. Winnipeg is fortunate. The city of Hamilton is fortunate. So is Victoria, British Columbia, and Dartmouth across the harbour from Halifax has its own golf course in the heart of the city. There are other cities as well which can offer this great attraction.
But some cities have seen their downtown golf courses go for housing development. I am thinking of Verdun. Only in the east end of Montreal, as I understand it, does there exist one municipal course. Otherwise people of that great metropolis have to drive many tens of miles before they reach a suitable course.
In the national capital area, Madam Speaker, one of the features which makes it such an attractive place, apart from yourself and some others in this chamber-one of the charms is the presence of a number of golf courses near at hand.
The reason I raised my question with the Minister of State for Urban Affairs was to get some declaration from
November 18, 1975

him that his department and CMHC would not try to take over such land for housing development if there were some guarantee that these courses would be open to the public, forming as they do an essential part of living in a highly civilized style.
I think it would be a terrible thing if all urban areas were simply block after block marching away into an indefinite distance of housing and buildings, without green space or other space for people to enjoy recreation. I hope that when a reply comes from the government there will be a recognition that spaces such as Ashburn should continue as recreational areas, and that the government will never stoop to the weapon of expropriation which is the only way Ashburn could possibly be taken for housing development, since the voting members would see to it otherwise that it was used as a golf course indefinitely.
But I am not thinking only of Ashburn. I am raising this as a larger issue looking ahead at how our cities will be 20, 50 or 100 years from now, and believing there ought to be something in government policy which acknowledges the need for these recreational areas.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Robert Gauthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: URBAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST CENTRAL MORTGAGE NOT BUY ASHBURN GOLF COURSE IN HALIFAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity this evening to reply in the name of my minister to the question asked by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) on November 14. He referred to the possible purchase of the Ashburn Golf Course in Halifax by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I wish to confirm information which I am sure the hon. member already has in his possession to the effect that the board of directors of the Ashburn Golf Course refused the corporation's offer. In the opinion of the board of directors of the golf course, the land was worth between $2.8 million and $3 million, a figure approximately double the price offered by CMHC. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is not interested in the purchase of this property at the price asked by its owners as it would necessitate a housing density too high to permit an appropriately sensitive development treatment of this attractive land.
If I may add a personal note, Madam Speaker, I know that officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are looking around Halifax for a suitable site for a housing development. I am sure the hon. member will understand that if CMHC tees off on this objective with its usual drive, it should go a "fairway" toward securing enough green to initiate an attractive and suitable housing development. Let us hope that there will not be too many slices or hooks in the process, and that all levels of government will "putt" forth their co-operation in bringing to Halifax a worth-while development financed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-UNITED NATIONS FORCE IN MIDDLE EAST-POSSIBILITY OF REQUEST FOR INCREASED CANADIAN COMMITMENT
NATIONAL DEFENCE-UNITED NATIONS FORCE IN MIDDLE EAST-POSSIBILITY OF REQUEST FOR INCREASED CANADIAN COMMITMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when on October 24 I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) if Canada had received any request for increased involvement in the Middle East peace
Adjournment Debate
forces of the UN, I had in mind the broadened UN role consequent upon the Sinai agreement between Egypt and Israel, and the UN security vote in reference thereto.
This was before the recent vote in the UN general assembly which has brought forth in some quarters strong anti-UN sentiments. There have been those so distressed by the vote on Zionism that they feel Canada, because of that vote, should turn its back upon the United Nations and cancel our membership. Others have suggested that we show our hostility to the resolution by refusing to allow into this country spokesmen for the Palestinian people. I would not for a moment seek to judge or appraise the motives of those who counsel such action, but I think these are times when UN supporters should express themselves.
Suggestions that a Palestinian spokesman be prevented from addressing a public meeting in Ottawa do little to enhance Canada's reputation as a democracy. If freedom of speech is to be restricted only to those with whom we agree, it is not freedom at all. The UN resolution on Zionism was unwise, unhelpful, and unnecessary, and it would have been far better had its sponsors dropped it. But many UN delegations viewed it otherwise.
In an earlier day the United States had no difficulty in commanding a majority on almost any General Assembly vote. This condition no longer prevails, and U.S. Ambassador Moynihan's recent comment that the "decent countries" were in the minority side was something less than helpful.
Equally wrong are the suggestions that Canada should, with petulant disdain, withdraw from the UN because the majority of its members supported resolutions we oppose. With all its failings and faults the UN is still indispensable. I well remember the words of that great gentleman, scholar and statesman who the minister will remember, Hon. J. M. MacDonnell, who after a visit to the world body said, "If this organization did not exist we would have to invent it".
Canada is not a combatant in the Middle East conflict. There is no need for us to be pro or anti Arab or Israeli. We claim to be on friendly terms with all. Under such circumstances it would seem unfair to deny a voice to a spokesman for the Palestinian side while welcoming all those who come as spokesmen for the Israeli cause. A million and a half Palestinians live in hopeless despair in refugee camps throughout the Middle East, driven from their homes nearly 30 years ago. They were not consulted when their lands were alienated from them. How cruel to deny them the right to speak as well.
Canada is a founding member of the United Nations, one with a good reputation there. Much of our good will and high regard stems from the fine work of the people who have served on various UN peacekeeping forces in many parts of the world over many years.
I hope that if and when a call comes from the UN it will be given a positive response. Tours of duty in these sensitive areas are not without hardships and difficulty. It is hard not to be convinced that our forces generally are being too long denied the kind of equipment their competence and their duty require. But their capacity to perform their role is widely acclaimed and I am proud of their good

November 18, 1975
Adjournment Debate
record as are the minister and his charming parliamentary secretary.
I hope, therefore, that we will follow the sane advice of Ambassador Rae and of the Ottawa Citizen, which in a recent editorial declared that hysterics are no help. I therefore invite a positive answer from the parliamentary secretary, and I assure her I will do my best to support efforts on behalf of the UN's continuing program to reduce tensions and inhibit the prospect for further explosions in sensitive areas of the world.

This being said, I think he will understand if I address myself more directly to the question under consideration, and that is no longer the possibility but the actual request for an increase in the Canadian commitment to UNEF's mandate.
The hon. member knows that four days after his question in the House on October 24, as a result of the renewal by the Security Council of UNEF's mandate involving an increase in the size of the force, a request was received from the Secretary General. subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ATTENDANCE OF CANADA AT RESTRICTED ECONOMIC SUMMIT MEETING IN FRANCE
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ATTENDANCE OF CANADA AT RESTRICTED ECONOMIC SUMMIT MEETING IN FRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 28 I put a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) as follows, and it is to be found at page 8604 of
Hansard:
Will the minister indicate if we have been invited to the restricted economic summit meeting in France in mid-November, bearing in mind that monetary questions are to be raised there? If not, will he explain why we have been snubbed when there will be nations in attendance that have less at stake than Canada?
The minister declined to answer, stating this was something to do with the Department of External Affairs. I then put the same question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), and his answer at that time was that the final decision had not been taken in respect of attendance at the summit, but Canada had expressed and was continuing to express its interest. He went on to state: The hon. member will recall that Canada has received quite important public support for its presence from the President of the United States and the Secretary of State. We are still awaiting a decision that we hope will make it possible for us to attend.

I am sorry the Secretary of State for External Affairs chose to leave the House rather than answer this question, just as he refused to answer the question of the speaker who preceded me.
This is an extremely important point. We now know that the conference was held last weekend and that the leaders of six major industrialized countries announced at the end of the three-day meeting that they had reached agreement on questions of world trade, monetary matters, and raw materials including energy. We also know Canada was not in attendance at the conference. We must ask ourselves in the name of Canada why that is so. We had the minister's word that the government hoped it would be possible for Canada to attend, so why were we refused?
We had more at stake, as I originally posed the question on October 28, than some of the nations that did attend, yet we were snubbed by these nations which chose to hold the meeting. I believe we must begin asking ourselves whether the government's past is catching up in terms of international affairs. Is the fact that we have been failing to live up to our commitments with such organizations as NATO now registering with these nations that state, "If you will not carry your load on economic matters you shall not have the political clout and voice you deem necessary"? I think the time has come when we must put the government on the spot.
In the early 1960's some 25 per cent of our federal spending was on defence, and today it is about 10 per cent. Our defence spending has slumped to 2 per cent of our gross national product, compared to 6 per cent in the United States and an average of over 4 per cent for major NATO countries. I suggest this policy has been shortsighted and we are now paying the price in loss of international credibility and stature.
The summit conference held in Paris was an important matter dealing with economic questions which the government has claimed have an influence in Canada. In fact up until recently the government stated that international conditions were the cause of inflation in this country and that there was little that could be done about that. Now we find the government is in the awkward position of not being invited to this important conference on international matters.
If I may I should like to point out that the snub we have received is possibly due to the widespread feeling among these NATO countries that Canada wants defence on the cheap, with a political voice disproportionate to its contribution. At the NATO conference this fall our allies spoke scathingly of a country which was becoming a sponge within the alliance. One top NATO defence planner said Canada has been one of the weaker brethren, the weakest in fact after Luxembourg, since 1971 when we reduced our forces in Europe from 10,000 to 5,000.
I had hoped the Secretary of State for External Affairs would treat this matter with such importance that he would reply this evening. I am disappointed that he is not here. I believe this is a very important matter. It is important, if in truth the government believes in an anti-inflationary program, that it project itself into the international scene where our voice will be heard on the matters dealt with at the Paris summit. It is not enough to receive an official communique or whatever the government has
November 18, 1975

received concerning that summit. Our ministers should have been in attendance. They know they should have been in attendance. I hope there will be an explanation concerning why we have received this rebuke at the hands of nations which ordinarily we have looked upon as our allies.
We are a big nation. It is time the government projected us on to the world stage as what we are, a significant nation and not one that will accept paltry communiques from those who have made the decisions without having our counsel. I want an explanation, and every member of this House deserves an explanation.

speakeroldname: Miss Monique Begin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ATTENDANCE OF CANADA AT RESTRICTED ECONOMIC SUMMIT MEETING IN FRANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, may I first state that I understood the tradition in this House to be that parliamentary secretaries assist their ministers in answering questions which are dealt with at this late hour of the day. I might also add that the minister might have been quite surprised to hear about the relationship between the Rambouillet summit and our contribution to NATO. I should like to make it quite clear that France did not refuse the attendance of Canada at Rambouillet. We simply were not invited. This is quite a different matter.
If the hon. member opposite were more familiar with the defence budget of NATO I believe he would know that the
Adjournment Debate
position of France regarding NATO would not, in the logic he used, have the consequence of excluding Canada from the Rambouillet conference. Having said this may I remind my colleague opposite that the minister stated more than once in the House that should Canada not be invited to the Rambouillet conference "it would not be helpful"-and I am using his words-and "it would not have a favourable effect on our bilateral position." This is pretty obvious, but it does not mean we take it as a provocation. We hope that our bilateral relations will develop in harmony more and more week after week. We thought it would be very important for Canada to participate in the Paris summit.
The matter at hand involved national and international economic interests. In our estimation, our national and international interests warranted our presence, even though the Canadian market represents only about 22 million inhabitants and cannot compare with the European Community or with Japan. But, the point of view of the host country, the hon. member will recall, I think, was to keep the group of participants to a very limited number.
Still the results of the conference seem very positive and as soon as Canada will have the opportunity to analyse the reports, it will divulge its views on each point on which agreement was reached.
